items.body:
Der Digitalpakt 2.0 ist gestartet, doch in vielen Ländern stehen die Förderrichtlinien noch aus. Was sollten Schulen und Schulträger jetzt tun? Livia Brenner, Projektleiterin Förderprogramme der Digitalakademie von Converge Germany, über die Lehren aus dem ersten Digitalpakt, die Rolle der Fortbildung und den Wert einer ehrlichen Bestandsaufnahme.

**Frau Brenner, der Digitalpakt 2.0 ist seit September in Kraft. Was ändert sich für Schulen und Schulträger?**

Beim ersten Digitalpakt ging es vor allem darum, die Schulen überhaupt auszustatten, also mit WLAN, Endgeräten und Präsentationstechnik. Das ist an vielen Schulen gelungen. Heute lautet die Frage eher: Wie halten wir die Technik am Laufen? Wie erneuern wir sie? Und wie kommt sie wirklich im Unterricht an?

Genau hier setzt der neue Pakt an. Bund und Länder stellen bis 2030 zusammen fünf Milliarden Euro bereit. Gefördert werden weiterhin Netzwerke, WLAN, Endgeräte und Lernplattformen. Neu dazu kommen digitale Bildungsinhalte und Software für den Unterricht. Auch der Aufbau professioneller Strukturen für Administration und Support ist förderfähig, ebenso Fortbildungen für Lehrkräfte. Außerdem sollen die Verfahren einfacher werden, etwa durch Pauschalen. Was davon Vorrang hat und wie die Verfahren konkret aussehen, entscheidet allerdings jedes Bundesland selbst.

**Das heißt, Schulen und Schulträger müssen erst einmal abwarten?**

Beim Geld ja, bei der Vorbereitung nicht. Viele Länder arbeiten noch an ihren Richtlinien. Die Zeit bis dahin lässt sich aber gut nutzen. Wer weiß, wo er steht und was er braucht, kann schnell handeln, sobald die Regeln feststehen. Wer erst dann anfängt, über seinen Bedarf nachzudenken, verliert Monate.

**Sie sprechen für die Digitalakademie von Converge Germany. Was genau macht sie?**

Die Digitalakademie ist der Fortbildungsanbieter von Converge Germany. Converge Germany selbst ist ein IT-Systemhaus und arbeitet seit mehr als 20 Jahren mit Schulen, Schulträgern und Behörden zusammen. Mit seinem 360°-Ansatz deckt das Unternehmen alles ab, von Planung und Beschaffung über die IT-Infrastruktur bis zu Service und Support im laufenden Betrieb. Wir in der Digitalakademie sorgen dafür, dass all das im Klassenzimmer ankommt.

Unser Team arbeitet bundesweit. Die Referent*innen haben einen pädagogischen oder bildungswissenschaftlichen Hintergrund, und einige haben selbst unterrichtet, ich selbst auch. Wir haben insgesamt bereits über 100.000 Lehrkräfte fortgebildet. Diese Nähe zur Praxis merkt man in jeder Fortbildung. Wir kennen den Moment, in dem 28 Augenpaare gespannt nach vorne schauen und die Technik streikt. Und wir wissen auch, dass im Lehrerzimmer selten Zeit bleibt, sich in ein neues Programm einzuarbeiten.

**Sie haben Schulen und Schulträger schon beim ersten DigitalPakt begleitet. Was haben Sie daraus gelernt?**

Vor allem eines: Ausstattung allein reicht nicht. Wir haben in den vergangenen Jahren sehr unterschiedliche Projekte umgesetzt. Für einen Kunden haben wir eine Cloud-Lösung aufgebaut, über die rund 25.000 Lehrkräfte-Geräte zentral verwaltet und abgesichert werden. Bei einem anderen haben wir das WLAN im gesamten Schulumfeld eingerichtet, ausgelegt für rund 135.000 Nutzerinnen und Nutzer.

Dabei hat sich ein Muster gezeigt. Gut lief es dort, wo Technik, Support und Fortbildung von Anfang an zusammen geplant wurden. Wo das nicht der Fall war, standen Geräte ungenutzt im Schrank – oder die Lehrkräfte wurden zu Hobby-Administratoren.

Ein Beispiel ist mir besonders im Gedächtnis geblieben. An einer Schule reichte das WLAN nicht aus, um die Updates für die iPads aufzuspielen. Eine Lehrerin hat deshalb jeden Tag Geräte aus dem iPad-Koffer mit nach Hause genommen, damit sie dort die Updates laden konnten. Das zeigt großes Engagement. Aber so etwas darf nicht die Lösung sein.

**Stichwort Fortbildung: Im Digitalpakt 2.0 ist sie förderfähig. Was bedeutet das für Schulen?**

Zunächst ist das ein wichtiges Signal. Der Pakt erkennt an, dass Technik ohne Qualifizierung wenig bewirkt. Wie die Länder Fortbildung umsetzen, ist unterschiedlich. Manche setzen stärker auf ihre Landesinstitute, andere binden externe Anbieter ein. Oft ergänzt sich beides. Wir arbeiten zum Teil auch mit Landesinstituten zusammen, etwa in Rheinland-Pfalz. Viele Schulen kommen aber direkt auf uns zu, weil sie ein Angebot suchen, das genau zu ihrer Ausstattung und ihrem Kollegium passt.

Was konkret über den Digitalpakt finanziert wird, legt jedes Land in seiner Richtlinie fest. Bis dahin lohnt es sich, den eigenen Fortbildungsbedarf zu klären. Dabei unterstützen wir Schulen und schauen gemeinsam, welche Förderwege infrage kommen. Neben dem Digitalpakt gibt es oft weitere Programme, die sich gut kombinieren lassen.

**Schauen wir auf den Unterricht selbst: Was ist beim digitalen Lehren und Lernen aus Ihrer Sicht entscheidend?**

Pädagogik und Didaktik müssen vorne stehen. Die erste Frage sollte nie lauten: Welches Tool nehmen wir? Sie sollte lauten: Was sollen die Schüler*innen lernen, und wie können digitale Medien sie dabei unterstützen? Das klingt banal, wird im Alltag aber oft umgekehrt gemacht.

Dazu kommt Zeit. Kollegien brauchen Raum, um Neues auszuprobieren und sich auszutauschen. Schon eine einzelne Fortbildung kann manchmal einiges anstoßen. Nachhaltig wird es aber dann, wenn eine Schule ein gemeinsames Zielbild hat und Schritt für Schritt daran arbeitet.

Lehrkräfte sollten dabei keine Systemadministratoren sein müssen. Wenn das WLAN streikt oder die Geräte nicht synchronisieren, kostet das Unterrichtszeit und Nerven. Ein verlässlicher Support durch einen starken IT-Partner ist deshalb auch eine pädagogische Frage.

**Gerade künstliche Intelligenz verunsichert viele Lehrkräfte. Was brauchen sie?**

items.subtitle: Wissenschaftskommunikation ist politischer geworden und muss sich in einer zunehmend polarisierten Welt behaupten.

items.body:
Wissenschaftskommunikation ist politischer geworden und muss sich in einer zunehmend polarisierten Welt behaupten. Annette Leßmöllmann und Markus Weißkopf sprechen zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de über Erfolge, Herausforderungen und notwendigen Wandel.

Am 24. November 2016 ging Wissenschaftskommunikation.de online. In unserem [Schwerpunkt zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wo-steht-die-wisskomm/)blicken wir auf prägende Entwicklungen zurück *und fragen, wo die Wissenschaftskommunikation heute steht.*

**Mit welcher Idee und welchem persönlichen Anspruch seid Ihr 2016 an der Gründung von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de beteiligt gewesen?**

**Markus Weißkopf** ist Redakteur des Research.Table bei Table.Media. Er war Geschäftsführer von Wissenschaft im Dialog und hat dort unter anderem die Plattform Wissenschaftskommunikation.de aufgebaut. Foto: WiD

Markus Weißkopf: Kurz zuvor hatten Wissenschaft im Dialog und der Bundesverband Hochschulkommunikation gemeinsam die [Leitlinien zur guten Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/leitlinien-zur-guten-wissenschaftskommunikation-85129/) veröffentlicht. In dem Zuge hatte die Community viel über gemeinsame Werte, aber auch über die Professionalisierung der Wissenschaftskommunikation diskutiert. Wissenschaftskommunikation.de sollte unter anderem eine Plattform für diese Themen bieten.

Annette Leßmöllmann: Die Plattform sollte zeigen: Wissenschaftskommunikation bedeutet mehr als nur Pressemitteilungen und Hochglanzmagazine. Mir war es ein Anliegen, Forschung und Praxis zusammenzubringen und somit die [Vermittlung der Wissenschaftskommunikationsforschung](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/kategorie/forschung/) voranzutreiben. Zum einen, um praxisrelevante Ergebnisse bekannt zu machen, zum anderen, um die theoretische Weiterentwicklung, die Interdisziplinarität und die Selbstreflexion des Forschungsfeldes zu zeigen. Gleichzeitig sollten Praxisfragen für die Forschung nachvollziehbar werden, um neue Forschung anzustoßen.

**Annette Leßmöllmann** (@annetteless.bsky.social) ist promovierte Linguistin und hat am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT)* den Lehrstuhl für Wissenschaftskommunikation mit dem Schwerpunkt Linguistik inne. Sie lehrt in den Bachelor- und Master-Studiengängen „Wissenschaft – Medien – Kommunikation“ (@WMKstudium).

**Welche Fragen oder Konfliktlinien aus der Gründungszeit beschäftigen die Community bis heute?**

Weißkopf: „Als Anlaufstelle Nr. 1 hat sich das Online-Lexikon Wikipedia im Internet längst etabliert. Die Wissenschaft sollte das Potenzial von Wikipedia für die Vermittlung fundierten Wissens ernsthaft prüfen.“ Das hat eine Pressesprecherin [im Rahmen des ersten Schwerpunkts „Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation“](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/blick-nach-vorn-wie-sieht-die-wissenschaftskommunikation-der-zukunft-aus-5-13517/) geschrieben. Natürlich ist das Prüfen wissenschaftsimmanent. Aber im Bereich der Kommunikation können wir es uns nicht erlauben, jahrelang zu prüfen. Die Wissenschaft hat nun ein Engagement bei oder für [Wikipedia](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/format/wikipedia/) so lange geprüft, bis es zu spät war. Nur einzelne Einrichtungen wie die Universität Innsbruck bilden hier Ausnahmen. Da würde ich mir manchmal mehr Mut zum Experimentieren wünschen!

Leßmöllmann: Was sich bereits vor zehn Jahren angekündigt hat: Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden. Dass sie in Interessenslagen und Machtstrukturen eingebettet ist und dass es als machtvoller kommunikativer Akt angesehen wird, wenn jemand „bestimmt“, was wahr oder falsch ist – das war damals eher ein Gedankenexperiment, ist heute aber deutlich als Konflikt zu spüren.

Es wird für die Wissenschaftskommunikation viel schwieriger, wenn es den Entscheider*innen reicht, dass sich etwas wahr anfühlt, auch wenn es nicht wahr ist. Dass etwa politische und gesellschaftliche Entscheidungen gegen den vorherrschenden wissenschaftlichen Konsens getroffen werden, ist angesichts der Klimakrise deutlich bedrohlicher und krisenhafter spürbar als noch vor zehn Jahren.

### „Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden.“

Annette Leßmöllmann

**Direkt mit dem ersten Schwerpunkt des Portals haben wir damals auf die** **[Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/zukunft-der-wissenschaftskommunikation/)** **geblickt. Welche damaligen Hoffnungen und Befürchtungen haben sich aus Eurer Sicht bewahrheitet und welche nicht?**

Leßmöllmann: Es hat sich die Hoffnung bewahrheitet, dass heute stärker darauf geachtet wird, Kommunikationsaktivitäten wissenschaftlich fundiert zu evaluieren. Zudem hat es funktioniert, dass sich die Community intensiver vernetzt und dass Forschung und Praxis enger zusammenarbeiten.

Es gab auch den Wunsch, dass Wissenschaftskommunikation stärker Teil der Gesellschaft und des täglichen Austauschs über die relevanten Themen der Zeit wird. In einem Aspekt hat sich der Wunsch bewahrheitet, allerdings anders als gedacht: Durch [generative Künstliche Intelligenz](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/themen/kuenstliche-intelligenz/) sind Wissen und Wissenschaft jetzt noch einfacher und dialogischer zu erreichen.

Gleichzeitig wurde die DIN-Norm der Kommunikation aufgeweicht: Es ist nicht mehr sicher, ob das Kommunizierte auch stimmt. Dies trägt zu einer Wissenskrise bei. Etwas dystopisch und pointiert formuliert: Gesagt und geglaubt wird, was gut klingt und auf die Interessen der eigenen Peer Group einzahlt. Das zeigt, dass wir in einer völlig anderen Welt als vor zehn Jahren leben. Die Rolle des Wissens, die demokratische Verankerung und die Wissenschaftsfreiheit stehen zur Debatte.

## The Fall of the House of Usher , The Tell-Tale Heart , and More">25 Films Inspired by Edgar Allan Poe Online: The Fall of the House of Usher , The Tell-Tale Heart , and More

in Film , Literature | November 24th, 2026 Leave a Comment

-->

Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and sev­er­al adap­ta­tions of “The Fall of the House of Ush­er” will almost cer­tain­ly come near the top. At first glance, that sto­ry of a man pay­ing a vis­it to an old friend who lives with his twin sis­ter in their fam­i­ly’s grand house — each of the lat­ter three well advanced into a dif­fer­ent process of dete­ri­o­ra­tion — might seem too short, as well as too light on con­flict to trans­late into a con­ven­tion­al screen­play. Yet it’s also full of cin­e­mat­i­cal­ly irre­sistible images, from the some­how ruinous yet whol­ly intact tit­u­lar man­sion to the blood­i­ly wretched sis­ter throw­ing her­self upon the ter­ri­fied broth­er who entombed her alive while their ances­tral home col­laps­es around them.

Of the twen­ty or thir­ty ver­sions of “The Fall of the House of Ush­er” so far made for the screen, the most cel­e­brat­ed remains the one Jean Epstein direct­ed in 1928. Offi­cial­ly des­ig­nat­ing it as one of the “great movies,” Roger Ebert calls that pic­ture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunt­ing spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast mar­ble expanse, inter­rupt­ed here and there by an item of fur­ni­ture that seems dwarfed by the sur­round­ing empti­ness. An odd stair­case ris­es from one dis­tant cor­ner. It is not impos­si­ble that this vision, in one of the best-known French sur­re­al­ist films, inspired the design­ers of the great hall of Xanadu in Cit­i­zen Kane .”

The avant-garde film­mak­ing duo James Sib­ley Wat­son Jr. and Melville Web­ber (in col­lab­o­ra­tion with e. e. cum­mings, who con­tributed to the script) could hard­ly man­age the same scale of pro­duc­tion design for their own short adap­ta­tion of Poe’s sto­ry , which hap­pened to come out the same year.

But the result­ing Expres­sion­ist take on the mate­r­i­al has also been high­ly acclaimed, and through this YouTube playlist of Poe films , you can expe­ri­ence not just both of them, but also oth­er adap­ta­tions of “The Fall of the House of Ush­er” by idio­syn­crat­ic Czech ani­ma­tor Jan Švankma­jer and B‑movie pow­er­house Roger Cor­man . Sen­si­tive to Poe’s sen­sa­tion­al­ist appeal and air of trans­gres­sive deca­dence, Cor­man end­ed up direct­ing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” near­ly all of which star Vin­cent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more close­ly asso­ci­at­ed with Poe than Price, a link Tim Bur­ton cel­e­brat­ed in ani­ma­tion at the begin­ning of his career. Price even played the writer him­self in An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe , a spe­cial from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amon­til­la­do,” “The Pit and the Pen­du­lum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapt­ed Poe sto­ry of them all, also appears on the playlist in var­i­ous forms: an ear­ly D. W. Grif­fith fea­ture , the direc­to­r­i­al debut of Jules Dassin , an ani­mat­ed short nar­rat­ed by James Mason , a British psy­cho­log­i­cal thriller , and a trans­po­si­tion into mod­ern-day New Orleans . And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watch­ing through all 25 of these films, con­sid­er watch­ing the recent, well-received Fall of the House of Ush­er minis­eries on Net­flix — an enter­tain­ment plat­form that sat­is­fies much the same appetites Poe’s sto­ries have been feed­ing for near­ly two cen­turies.

items.body:
A long journey from Tokyo to the island of Naoshima to see art gave Jemal Inaishvili, a shipping executive and collector, an idea for how he might convince people to make a similar trek within his home country of Georgia in the South Caucasus. Unlike visiting Naoshima, which typically involves a full day of travel, the drive from the capital city of Tbilisi to Kakheti, Georgia’s eastern wine region, is around two hours, three in heavy traffic. “Of course, I cannot copy them,” he told me recently, “but I will do something similar, but based on Georgian art.”

The result is the Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art, which opened to the public earlier this month on land Inaishvili bought a decade ago for a small winery. The site now also holds a hotel, a sculpture park, and a red-slatted museum with a rooftop for performances and film screenings by the Tbilisi practice Midamo. This admission-free venue will stage four exhibitions a year, drawing from Inaishvili’s collection of about 1,000 works.

To lead the programming, Inaishvili has hired 28-year-old Nino Sulkhanishvili. “Sometimes one’s experience will be the barrier,” he said of the creative director, who is in her first institutional role. “Together with the foundation, she is also growing.”

In heading up a private museum, Sulkhanishvili sees her role as helping to give Georgian artists the infrastructure to exhibit at home, like Elene Chantladze, whose solo show will open at the Kvareli Foundation in February. Such a setting, Sulkhanishvili said, “is extremely important, especially in your own country. … I feel Georgian artists deserve much more.” Location, too, matters: “contemporary art needs to be decentralized,” she said, noting the foundation’s aim to create an art ecosystem by bringing schoolchildren to visit and training local guides. A residency for both local and international artists will launch next year.

But Georgian art won’t be the foundation’s only focus after the first two years. The collection also includes work by Ukrainian, Turkish, and Armenian artists, which will be shown in the future. In the years to come, Sulkhanishvili hopes to build exchanges with neighboring and post-Soviet countries before looking further afield. “We really want to be a beacon within the region,” she said.

Installation view of “Georgian Contemporary Art: Origins and Continuities,” 2026, at Kvareli Foundation.

Photo Sera Dzneladze/Courtesy Kvareli Foundation

The inaugural exhibition, “Georgian Contemporary Art: Origins and Continuities” (on view through January 15), came together only six months before opening. Instead of just focusing solely on Inaishvili’s collection, Sulkhanishvili proposed a historical survey of the artists who worked outside the Soviet era’s state-sanctioned socialist realism. The show gathers 57 artists from the 1960s to the present, with roughly half the works from his collection and the rest on loan. “Even in the national museums, you don’t see everything together,” Sulkhanishvili said of the artists on view, many of whom are still often “excluded from the [official] narrative” of this moment in Georgian history. This time around, socialist realist artists are intentionally left out.

Irena Popiashvili, the dean of the Visual Arts, Architecture and Design School at Tbilisi’s Free University, said the importance of a show like this could not be understated when state museums often only focus a handful of national artists, like Georgia’s most celebrated painter Niko Pirosmani. “As an educator, it’s important for me, for example, to refer my students [to this show] and for them to be able to see the continuation of the Georgian art history, 20th century throughout and the beginning of the 21st,” she said.

Ushangi Khumarashvili, Abstraction, 1998.

Private Collection

The survey begins with the Thaw that followed Stalin’s death in 1953, when socialist realism remained doctrine but foreign magazines, like ARTnews and Art in America, trickled in. A pioneering figure of Abstract Expressionism in Georgia, Shura Bandzeladze saw a black-and-white reproduction of a Jackson Pollock in Art in America and took it as proof he was “on the right track,” according to Sulkhanishvili.

The risks of deviating from socialist realism were real, though. Ushangi Khumarashvili, a set designer from Kakheti’s largest city, Telavi, clashed with his director and was sent to a psychiatric hospital. On his release, he burned his earlier work and turned to abstraction. In 1974, non-conformist painter and graphic artist Otar Chkhartishvili took part in the unapproved avant-garde Bulldozer Exhibition in Moscow, which the authorities violently broke up. In Levan Chogoshvili’s painting 1924 (ca. 1980s), a dog carries a severed human hand, an image drawn from his grandmother’s account of Bolshevik executions, an episode that official Soviet histories left out. In an officially atheist country, even a return to earlier Western art traditions and the Christian themes they drew on could be equally dangerous. In 1978, Irakli Parjiani began writing out the Gospels by hand and illustrating them in the manner of medieval manuscripts, which Popiashvili described as “a revolutionary act.”

Levan Chogoshvili, 1924, ca. 1980s.

Courtesy the artist

items.title: What Schools Still Don’t Teach About Interest Rates and Why It Matters
items.subtitle: A savings account turns abstract lessons into something you can see each month.
items.feedText: Most people leave school able to calculate interest on paper. Far fewer leave knowing what interest will do to their lives. That gap is easy to miss because it doesn’t show up on a report card. It shows up years later, in loan papers, credit card statements and savings balances that never seem to grow. items.body:
# What Schools Still Don’t Teach About Interest Rates and Why It Matters | TeachThought

Most people leave school able to calculate interest on paper. Far fewer leave knowing what interest will do to their lives. That gap is easy to miss because it doesn’t show up on a report card. It shows up years later, in loan papers, credit card statements and savings balances that never seem to grow.

The problem isn’t that schools ignore math. Interest is taught as a formula, and the formula stops at the edge of the worksheet. Students learn how to find an answer but not how to read the numbers that will shape what they borrow, what they save and what they can afford. To close that gap, it helps to look at what gets left out, starting with how the subject is framed in the first place.

### The Gap Between Arithmetic and Everyday Money

### Formulas Without Consequences

A typical lesson on interest gives students a principal, a rate and a time period, then asks them to solve for the total. It’s tidy and it can be graded. It also hides almost everything that matters. Real rates change. Real balances get added to and drawn down. Real people make choices partway through, and those choices change the outcome.

When interest only ever appears as a problem with one right answer, students learn to treat it as a puzzle rather than as a force acting on their money every day.

### Interest Is a Price

The simplest idea missing from many classrooms is also the most useful one. Interest is the price of money over time. When you borrow, you pay that price. When you save, someone pays it to you. Once students see interest as a price, they start asking the questions they would ask about any purchase. Is this a good deal? Can I find it cheaper somewhere else? What happens if I wait?

That shift in thinking matters most when you see how interest builds over long stretches of time.

### How Compounding Actually Feels Over Time

### The Slow Start That Fools People

Compounding means you earn interest on your interest. Most students can repeat that definition. What they rarely get is a feel for how lopsided the results are.

Put $1,000 in an account earning 5% a year and leave it alone. In the first year, you earn $50. Nothing to get excited about. By year 30, the balance has grown to about $4,322, and that single year alone adds more than $200. The growth was always there, but it took decades to become obvious. People who expect fast results often give up during the slow early years, which is exactly when patience pays off most.

A quick shortcut called the rule of 72 makes this easier to grasp. Divide 72 by the interest rate, and you get a rough idea of how many years it takes money to double. At 6%, that’s about 12 years. A tool like the compound interest calculator on the SEC’s Investor.gov site lets students test different rates and time frames and watch the curve bend upward.

### Compounding Runs in Both Directions

The same math that rewards savers punishes borrowers. A credit card charging 24% APR works out to about 2% a month. On a $3,000 balance, that’s roughly $60 in interest in the first month. If you pay $75, only $15 actually goes toward what you owe. The balance barely moves, and the card company is happy to keep it that way.

Students who understand this early tend to treat credit cards very differently. Still, knowing how compounding works is only half the picture. The other half is knowing which rate you’re actually dealing with.

### Why the Rate You See Is Rarely the Rate You Pay

### APR, APY and the Fine Print

Banks and lenders use different terms for a reason. APR, or annual percentage rate, is often used for loans and doesn’t always show the effect of compounding. APY, or annual percentage yield, does. A 12% APR compounded monthly actually costs about 12.68% over a year. The gap looks small until it’s multiplied across a large balance or a long loan.

Few students are ever shown these two terms side by side. As a result, many adults compare offers without realizing they’re comparing different measurements.

### Inflation Eats Quietly

Even a correct rate can mislead you if inflation is ignored. If your savings earn 1% while prices rise 3%, your balance goes up but what it can buy goes down. Economists call the difference the real return. The Consumer Price Index published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics is the standard way to track how fast prices are rising, and checking it against your savings rate is a sobering exercise.

That raises a fair question. If rates matter this much, who decides what they are?

### Where Rates Come From

### The Central Bank’s Role

Rates don’t appear out of nowhere. In the United States, the Federal Reserve sets a target range for the federal funds rate , which is what banks charge each other for overnight loans. That rate ripples outward into mortgages, car loans, credit cards and savings accounts.

### Why Your Rate Moves, or Doesn’t

Some rates follow the Fed closely. Variable credit card rates often rise within weeks of a hike. Others lag behind or barely move at all. Many large banks are slow to raise what they pay savers, even when borrowing costs climb. Knowing this helps people spot when they’re being underpaid and gives them a reason to act. The easiest place to put that knowledge to work is a savings account.

### Savings Accounts as a Practical Classroom

### Watching Interest Work in Real Time

A savings account turns abstract lessons into something you can see each month. Deposits go in, interest gets added and the balance changes without any effort. For a young person, watching even a few dollars of interest arrive can make compounding feel real in a way no textbook can. It also builds a habit, and habits tend to outlast lessons.

Savings accounts carry little risk, too. Deposits at insured banks are protected up to set limits, which makes them a calm place to learn how rates behave before moving on to investments that can lose value.

items.body:
My mother tongue is Thai, but for a long time I couldn’t swear in Thai. That was because the international school I went to banned us from speaking Thai on campus. *No native languages, all the better to improve our English*. It was quite a colonial relationship. I remember the colonial roots of my English every time an American complements my fluency, now that I live in the US.

Because of the school ban my Thai was polite, sweet, but not cool. I had no slang. I could not swear. This changed in the last two years of high school. I did the International Baccalaureate, which then required fifty hours of service from each student in order to graduate with the IB diploma. That seemed like a lot of hours to me! I remember my reluctance to leave the beautiful school campus with its duck ponds and Thai sala and venture into the great unknown of the Klong Toei slums.

I was matched to work in an orphanage of kids with HIV. I squeal for babies and toddlers, and was thrilled. Thailand was early to destigmatize HIV/AIDS. I ended up spending years in this orphanage, holding babies with many wonderful volunteers. What bliss, truly. I learned the carrot dance that the toddlers were obsessed with then; I can still sing it. Then, to my chagrin, I was moved out of the baby and toddler center to be with the adolescents. I think there was some glamour to having an international school student among the older kids. I sensed status in their jostling to speak with me. When the teenagers heard me speak, they fell over themselves laughing. How did I sound like such a child! They taught me to swear. We spoke in slang. In my time in Klong Toei, my Thai finally entered adolescence.

I learned a lot in those fifty hours of volunteer service, which I ended up exceeding. First, service feels wonderful. Maybe in the very beginning it was uncomfortable because of self-consciousness—and who could be more self-conscious than a teenager. But even adolescent me was able to relax the *certainty that everyone was judging her* and enjoy the camaraderie. I brought candy, and we’d walk around in a big pack of teenagers through the slum.

I learned that when the rains come, the slum is first to flood and last to drain; I learned it loses power all the time; I learned that people can be proud of where they’re from even when home is a shack made from corrugated tin. I learned that phad thai is best made on a street-side wok; I learned that Muay Thai keeps kids, especially boys, out of trouble. I learned that no one begs nor steals if they can help it; I learned that people are generally kind and keen for friendship. It was a life-changing year, as it was meant to be.

Reflecting back on that period, I am struck by how effective it was to have a service requirement. We studied economics in IB and learned about purchasing power parity, which is the relative cost of a Big Mac in Cambodia, say, versus the US. But walking those streets, paying for food, looking away as buddies fished coins out of pockets, the cut-open plastic water bottles used to beg, and drains—that was a different education in the cost of living. Knowledge moved from head to heart.

Service can be a force-function to generosity. Some of us are born with access to our tender and generous nature; some of us have quite a crust around the heart. For whatever reasons (the causes and conditions of [karma](https://tricycle.org/buddhism-dharma/#samsara-karma-rebirth)) many of us have learned to armor the heart.

All of us are affected by culture, which is a collective karma. Thailand has a collective culture of generosity. It is startling and real. Don’t worry—there’s a shadow side to Thai culture too. I wrote a whole novel to process it.

The culture of the United States is not what I would call an open and generous one. There seems to be fear around opening the heart. It sounds like: *If I’m generous, someone will take advantage of me.*

It’s probably a well-earned fear. But we cannot begin to walk the path of a [bodhisattva](https://tricycle.org/glossary/bodhisattva/) without *dana*, generosity.

We cannot begin to walk the path of a bodhisattva without *dana*, generosity.

In the temple where I teach, students have asked what you should do if you can’t just produce generosity. What then?

It’s a brave question to voice in a room. This is the answer: Force-function generosity with service. Find a way to log fifty hours of service, and the generosity will be there in your heart by the end of that time.

We remain stuck in spiritual adolescence if we have not had a significant period of service and generosity in our lives. Spiritual adolescence is a preoccupation with comfort and status. It can last our whole life if we let it.

If you are ready to progress to adulthood, I recommend engaging in service. Letting go of individual protectiveness, and feeling the wide river of the heart’s flow is actually a relief. It is freeing in and of itself (though it is not Enlightenment). Push the edges of your comfortable existence and commit significant hours to service. It will widen the aperture of your heart and bring flow again. In Thai the word “kindness” literally means “water of the heart.” My mother tongue is wise. Kindness does flow. It arises naturally, without effort. Giving comes naturally, without effort. When there is flow. If there isn’t flow, we have to poke a hole in the armor of the heart. You poke a hole through service.

If you’ve traveled to developing countries from the US, you might have noticed the baseline generosity of most people. One reason for this is because people from a poor place have had to take responsibility for collective well-being. When you are from a poor country, you *know* that no one is coming to bail you out. Here in the US we might have a fantasy of FEMA or the President or the National Guard coming to people’s aid.

items.body:
First released in 2013, [Audient](https://musictech.com/brands/audient/)’s iD series is well-tailored to a wide range of applications and users: home and project [studios](https://musictech.com/tag/studios/), mobile systems, as an audio hub for podcasting, and even in broadcasting.

When rumours began swirling about a 2026 refresh to the product line, I expected some cosmetic tweaks and a few dBs of improvement in performance specs, as is typical for [interface](https://musictech.com/tag/audio-interfaces/) updates.

It turns out I was wrong; as Audient’s chief product officer Andy Allen explains: “iD [MK3] is a completely new technology platform built on our Analogue Intelligence Platform”.

- Editor’s Pick: [Audient smashes its way into the high-end interface market with Horizon](https://musictech.com/reviews/studio-recording-gear/audient-horizon-review/)

This new platform replaces the previous desktop units with four all-new propositions. For those buying their first studio-grade interface for a home setup, there’s iD2, and this will be joined in early 2027 by iD1 – look out for our review. Further up the scale, aimed at those who need higher input/output counts or a more advanced feature set, are iD2+ and iD4+, priced at £329 and £499, respectively. These are the two interfaces I’m testing here.

Audient iD2+. Image: Press

## What’s new in the iD2+ and iD4+?

All next-gen models retain a similar form factor to their predecessors, but the sleek, black, curvy look is starkly different to the previous hardware.

Replacing the per-channel controls is a more streamlined control panel with a rotary wheel. This new look brings iD’s design into line with Audient’s other modern interface families — the entry-level EVO and high-end [Horizon](https://musictech.com/reviews/studio-recording-gear/audient-horizon-review/) ranges.

I’m mourning the loss of individual channel controls, which now means you have to select a preamp before adjusting its settings. That said, the new design isn’t complex, and because channel gain is now controlled digitally, iD’s new Smartgain mitigates that stickiness.

I’m always dubious of auto-gain systems; they tend to be too conservative or finish their listening phase before fully sampling the dynamics of the source. But iD’s Smartgain lets you set the target level in 6dB steps from -18dBFS to -6dBFS, and set the listen time manually, so I actually find it useful.

The iD2+ provides two [mic](https://musictech.com/tag/microphones/)/line inputs, the first switchable to instrument mode by connecting a cable to the front-panel instrument input. There are four balanced line outputs plus an extremely punchy [headphone](https://musictech.com/tag/headphones/) output with 3.5mm and 6.35mm front sockets. Up to eight additional digital ins and outs can be handled thanks to an optical I/O pair that can operate in ADAT (multichannel) or S/PDIF (stereo) modes, and these are backed by a dedicated word clock output BNC, essential for sending iD’s digital sync to an external preamp with a digital output – Audient’s ASP880, for example.

iD4+ is slightly larger, with extra real estate accommodating an extra pair of mic/line input channels, an extra instrument input, and an additional 6.35mm headphone socket fed by its own bus and amp. A second optical pair ups the maximum digital channel count to 16.

Audient iD4+. Image: Press

## If it ain’t broke, make it better anyway

“The next-gen iD range [is built] around four things most interfaces in its class can’t offer,” says Allen, citing the “real analogue preamps” as the first example of this. Those preamps retain their design relationship to Audient’s ASP8024 mixing console, and offer a hefty 75dB of gain range, but Audient has thrown in a whole host of impressive additions.

Channels 1 and 2 of both units feature balanced insert points. The sheer usefulness of inserts is a hill I’ll die on — they’re so technically simple to implement I despair that so few interfaces have them. So bravo, Audient!

The analogue input channels’ high-pass filters now have variable cutoff frequency, sweepable from 20 Hz to 250 Hz, plus a variable phase shift dial that works in conjunction with the phase flip function, which is invaluable for dialling out phase problems when using multiple mics.

Analogue inputs also offer Analogue Tone Suite; a set of switchable tone-shaping tools combining analogue circuitry and DSP.

HMX engages a MOSFET circuit to add body and energy to a source, with a pleasing low-end warmth and saturation. It’s particularly useful for bringing weak-sounding kicks, basses and [guitars](https://musictech.com/tag/guitars/) to life, but can be a bit boomy if not used judiciously.

At the other end of the frequency scale, Lift is a DSP-based upper-mid-to-high [EQ](https://musictech.com/tag/eq/) boost to bring out detail and air. HMX and Lift can be enabled together with the Glow button, present on the hardware and in the iD Control software, or each can be enabled individually from the software.

Finally, there’s the Orbit impedance switching system. This provides three options, Punch, Smooth and Vintage, which correspond to input impedances of 2,800, 1,200 and 220 Ohms, respectively. Punch typically gives the cleanest, most responsive results, but the other options provide a welcome means of applying different colours and characters to an input.

items.body: Temporal coherence contributes to audiovisual speech perception, but how competing background noise affects perceived audiovisual synchrony remains unclear. This study examined whether signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) influences the width and midpoint of the perceived-synchrony interval during continuous audiovisual speech perception. Twenty-five adults with normal hearing and normal or corrected-to-normal vision were presented with Harvard/IEEE sentences spoken by a female talker and accompanied by eight-talker babble at −10, 0, and +10 dB SNR. Using a self-adjustment procedure, participants shifted the relative timing of the auditory and visual streams from audio-leading and visual-leading starting positions until the stimuli were perceived as synchronous. The difference between the resulting audio-leading and visual-leading adjustment endpoints defined the adjustment-derived temporal binding window (TBW), and their midpoint defined the point of subjective simultaneity (PSS). Results showed that the adjustment-derived TBW was significantly narrower at −10 dB SNR than at 0 or +10 dB SNR, whereas no significant difference was observed between the two higher SNR conditions. PSS did not differ significantly across SNR conditions. These findings suggest that adverse background noise can selectively constrain the temporal range over which audiovisual speech is perceived as simultaneous without producing a reliable shift in the temporal center of perceived simultaneity, highlighting the influence of listening conditions on audiovisual temporal perception during speech.

## Cheb Runner ~ 80K

The rhythmic skeletons of Ahwach, Gnawa and related musical traditions meet 808s, sampling and electronic production on Cheb Runner ‘s 80K , retaining their physical force even as their shapes change. The result feels rooted in a specific place while constantly pushing beyond it. This is sound that has no borders, in keeping with the ethos of Beat Machine Records.

That approach has deep roots in Reda Senhaji’s own musical history. In an interview with Giulio Pecci , Senhaji (aka Cheb Runner) recalls playing as a child in the streets of Ihchach in Agadir, making music from instruments, household objects and car parts, and later learning software in order to translate the rhythms he already had in his head into electronic form. He describes his tracks as emerging from street recordings, archived sounds and processed percussion before arriving at a “collision” with electronic music. 80K makes that collision tactile. This is music that nourishes the hair follicles of the skin.

On “Iznagn Engines”, rhythm seems almost motorised, its cyclical momentum generating heat ripples as acoustic and synthetic percussion rub against one another. “Azn Oudrar” opens the music outward without dissipating its tension, while “Gn-Awa” is all glistening friction, metallic percussion locking into an intoxicating, heliotropic pulsing that seems perpetually drawn towards greater intensity. Yet the density never becomes oppressive: the album’s sleek electronic production acts as a sonic nictitating membrane, softening the relentless polyrhythmic Gnawa beats without blunting their impact.

The 808 becomes crucial to this balancing act. As the liner notes stress, it operates as a “structural force rather than an accent”, something especially apparent on “Afouss Adar 808”, where the electronic low end doesn’t sit beneath the traditional rhythmic language so much as enter into it. This is precisely the question the album raises: whether the distinction between traditional percussion and the drum machine remains particularly useful when both are being made to participate in the same rhythmic system. “Tarwan Ganga” deepens the rhythm into an auburn haze, locking the listener into a meditative trance, before Guedra Guedra’s closing reworking of “Gn-Awa” opens up and lifts the source material into a dreamy, solar finale.

This is the second release in the Terra Tempo series, which Beat Machine Records describes as “redefining the boundaries of global sound by blending rich cultural heritage with the dynamic energy of modern club beats.” Although the album cover depicts a number of instruments that AI has kindly idenfied for me as the qraqeb, the guembri / sintir, the tallunt / allun, and possibly the naqus, 80K is far from an exercise in heritage preservation.

Speaking to Pecci, Cheb Runner describes Morocco as the endpoint of historical caravan routes and its rhythms as the product of a “multitude of tribes” and the interplay of cultures brought by migration. The album extends that process rather than merely representing it. The qraqeb, guembri, hand percussion, samples, machines and 808 belong to a continuum in which inherited forms remain alive precisely because they can be transformed. Intoxicating and intensely physical, 80K treats tradition as a living source of energy. ( Gianmarco Del Re )

items.body:
When I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community. Knowing there was a significant senior population here, I reached out to the town librarian with hopes of helping elders share their stories.

The local historical society took interest in this idea, which led to an exhibit at the 159-year-old Tunbridge World’s Fair, and a book series entitled *Folk Life: Tunbridge Oral Histories*. The first two print runs sold out. The second collection of stories has just been published, and people are already asking who will be featured in the third.

What is it about life stories that strikes such a universal chord? And why is it important—and even imperative—to share our stories with others? I interviewed oral historians, teachers, and a digital storyteller to discover more about why the age-old tradition of recording oral histories continues to make such a significant impact for individuals and communities.

## Fostering connections and reflection

Storytelling is, according to scientific research, a biological shortcut to human connection. [Uri Hasson](https://blog.ted.com/what-happens-in-the-brain-when-we-hear-stories-uri-hasson-at-ted2016/) and fellow researchers at Princeton University discovered that the brains of the storyteller and listener physically sync up while a story is being told, promoting social connection, trust, and empathy.

The more emotionally affecting the story is, the stronger this connection becomes. As emotions and tension rise, hormones are released, including oxytocin, the “bonding hormone”; dopamine, which sharpens focus; and cortisol, which promotes attention and alertness as conflicts in the story arise. These hormonal responses enhance both the listener’s memory and connection to the storyteller.

For Erin Barnaby, a digital storyteller and 11th-generation Tunbridge native, oral histories create a connection not only to people, but also time and place. “My dad recently sold his house to my uncle, a house that he built on land that my grandfather had given to him. I love to hear him tell stories about the shifting of the land, from sheep farms to dairy farms and the shift from open pastures to forests.”

Even when the subject matter might not be instantly relatable, the process of listening to another’s stories still creates a profound interpersonal connection. Esther Ehrlich, who worked at [UC Berkeley’s Oral History Center](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft/oral-history-center) for six years before launching an oral history business of her own, experienced this sense of connection firsthand:

> I was assigned an interview with a former medical malpractice insurance guy, which initially didn’t interest me at all. And then lo and behold, after interviewing this man, I found him absolutely fascinating. What I came to discover was that by the time we were done, or even partway in, I came to love every single person I interviewed. I would feel connected to them and them to me.

## Providing unique perspectives

From that biological and psychological basis, oral histories make a critical social contribution.

According to the [Oral History Association](https://oralhistory.org/), “oral history is the oldest type of historical inquiry, stemming from the oral traditions of myriad cultures across the globe, predating even the written word.” These personal stories expand upon the narratives of history books, allowing people from varied walks of life to share their unfiltered experiences and perspectives. Indeed, many works by trained historians rely on oral histories.

The founders of [Voice of Witness](https://voiceofwitness.org/), a nonprofit dedicated to advancing human rights by amplifying unheard voices, believe that oral history “can democratize history, contribute to narrative change, and illuminate issues and events in a profoundly powerful way.” Enabling individuals to safely share their stories opens people’s minds to fresh perspectives and vantage points.

While oral histories are limited to an individuals’ memories and are by nature subjective, they remain incredibly valuable in their ability to paint a portrait of time and place. Plus, their narrative-driven format brings history to life in a more memorable way than date- and fact-focused textbooks.

Helen Marks, a former history teacher who has spoken to thousands of students about her experience as a hidden child in Belgium during World War II, has observed that when a person shares their stories, it brings that part of history to life:

> I am among the few surviving hidden children who are willing and able to talk about their experiences in the Holocaust. Reading numbers on a page does not create the same impact as someone standing or sitting in front of you describing a moment that was frightening or was so foreign they didn’t know what to do.... I think that when you connect a face, no matter what the face looks like, you get a wholly different reaction than when you read a page full of facts.

## Leaving a legacy

Throughout the interviews I conducted for *Folk Life*, the importance of leaving a meaningful legacy was a common theme. “That’s the reason we share our stories,” says Marsha Higgins, a history teacher for nearly 40 years. “It makes us feel like we matter.”

Higgins taught students to create personal narratives from a young age. Decades later, former students still express their thanks for her guidance in teaching them the importance of recording their experiences.

“I encouraged students to write down things that happened to them. It’s helpful to know at the time, you’re creating chapters in your life, that your story is just as interesting as anybody else’s.”

Like Marks, Higgins grew up around immigrants from Europe. “And they all had stories,” she says. “Whenever we got together, somebody would tell me a story. How do you make conversation without one? It’s just so much a part of who we are.”

items.body:
**Mit dem XRecer XR1 tritt ein neuer Modeling-Verstärker und Multieffekt auf den Markt, der vorab bereits einige Vorschusslorbeeren einheimst. Die Ankündigung deutet auf ein leistungsstarkes und flexibles System hin und hört sich entsprechend vielversprechend an. Nun ist der Modeler des neuen chinesischen Herstellers vorbestellbar. Kommt hier die nächste Konkurrenz für Neural DSP und Line 6?**

## Üppige Ausstattung mit Octa-Core-Prozessor und 10-Zoll-Touchscreen

Dank leistungsstarker Prozessoren und der Unterstützung des NAM-A2-Formats verschwimmen die Grenzen zwischen den etablierten Platzhirschen von Fractal Audio, Kemper, Line 6, Neural DSP und Fender sowie der günstigeren Konkurrenz. Unter den zahlreichen neuen Produkten sticht insbesondere der XRecer XR1 hervor, der im bühnentauglichen Pedalboard-Format mit zwölf Fußschaltern und einem 10-Zoll-Touchscreen direkt klotzt statt zu kleckern. Angetrieben wird das System von einer leistungsstarken Octa-Core-CPU, ergänzt durch GPU und Neural Processing Unit (NPU). Hinzu kommt ein integriertes 16×16-USB-Audio-Interface.

Die Hersteller-Webseite zeigt eine Bedienoberfläche mit vier parallelen Signalwegen und jeweils acht Slots, die Platz für jede Menge Amps und Effekte bieten. Auch die Rückseite ist beeindruckend ausgestattet: Neben vier Instrumenteneingängen und einem Mikrofoneingang stehen symmetrische XLR- und Klinkenausgänge, zwei Expression-Pedal-Anschlüsse, zwei Effektschleifen sowie MIDI zur Verfügung. Ein Looper ist ebenfalls integriert.

## Modeling, Effekte und NAM-A2-Kompatibilität inklusive TONE3000-Anbindung

Die Kompatibilität zum Open-Source-Format NAM dürfte für etliche Musiker interessant sein, steht hier doch ein großer Fundus fertig erfasster Verstärker und anderer Sounds zur Verfügung. Der XR1 unterstützt neben älteren NAM-A1-Modellen auch NAM A2 Full und A2 Lite. Besonders interessant ist die direkte Integration der Tone-Library von TONE3000: Über das WLAN des Geräts lassen sich passende Profile durchsuchen und herunterladen, ohne dafür einen Computer bemühen zu müssen.

Dazu kommt das proprietäre Capture-Format CapX, mit dem sich eigene Verstärker und Pedale erfassen lassen. Außerdem bietet der XR1 zahlreiche Effekte und die Möglichkeit, Impulsantworten von Drittanbietern zu laden. Die integrierten Amp- und Effektmodelle ergänzen das Angebot. Laut Hersteller umfasst die Ausstattung unter anderem 50 Amp-Modelle, 13 Cabinet-Modelle und 111 Effektmodelle. Üppige Rigs und komplexe Effektkombinationen scheinen damit möglich. Dank der vier parallelen Signalwege lassen sich zudem mehrere Signalquellen innerhalb eines Presets bearbeiten.

## Preis und Verfügbarkeit

Mit dem XR1 dürfte der neue chinesische Hersteller XRecer ein heißes Eisen im Feuer haben. Nun darf man auf die klangliche Performance gespannt sein. Der XRecer XR1 lässt sich ab sofort im Musikhaus Thomann zu einem knackigen Preis von 1.399 Euro vorbestellen. Die Lieferzeit soll bei sechs bis acht Wochen liegen – etwas Geduld muss man also mitbringen.

Weitere Informationen unter: [https://www.xrecer.com/products/xr1](https://www.xrecer.com/products/xr1)

items.title: learning to move is how we first construct ourselves, and then everything around us
items.subtitle: Sometime in the fifth century B.C., Greek sculptors worked out a way to put motion into something that could not move.
items.feedText: Contrapposto, as Renaissance artists would later name it, describes a standing figure resting its weight on a single leg, allowing the hips, shoulders, and torso to tilt in opposing directions. items.body:
Sometime in the fifth century B.C., Greek sculptors worked out a way to put motion into something that could not move. Contrapposto, as Renaissance artists would later name it, describes a standing figure resting its weight on a single leg, allowing the hips, shoulders, and torso to tilt in opposing directions. Against the stiff, frontal poses of the Archaic statues that came before it, contrapposto introduced a frozen promise of movement.

In 1968, [Bruce Nauman](https://www.designboom.com/tag/bruce-nauman/) walked it. Hands clasped behind his neck, hips swaying, he carried the pose up and down a narrow wooden corridor in his studio. That single-channel video became the basis for a series he was still making half a century later, shown in 2021 at Punta della Dogana. What stayed with me was the scale: seven projections, each large enough to make a man in a T-shirt and jeans feel monumental, and the flesh-and-blood performers executing the exact instructions he had written at the end of the sixties.

Watching them inhabit those movements in the same room pulled Nauman’s interrogation of the body out of the abstract; you were no longer just observing a study of human nature from a distance, but suddenly conscious of your own weight and footing beside them. Curators Carlos Basualdo and Caroline Bourgeois described his original video as a confrontation with *‘the simple fact of learning to walk as our first real way of constructing ourselves.’* What is true of the body turns out to be true of almost everything built around it. We make ourselves by moving, and then we remake the world to suit the way we move.

Bruce Nauman, Contrapposto Studies III, 2015-2016 | via designboom’s article [↗ designboom.com](https://www.designboom.com/art/palazzo-grassi-bruce-nauman-archive-for-the-future-conversations-04-24-2021/)

Time itself was remade across entire countries to accommodate a new way of moving. Until the 1840s, every British town kept its own hours, read off its own sun: Oxford ran five minutes behind London, Carnforth eleven, Barrow nearly thirteen. Then the trains arrived, and the clocks had to agree. The Great Western Railway switched to ‘railway time’ in November 1840; the Railway Clearing House ordered Greenwich into every station in 1847; and by 1855, roughly 98 percent of British towns had surrendered their local noon. North America began coordinating its schedules only after two trains running on different clocks collided at Valley Falls in 1853, and it took another three decades to settle the matter nationally. Your phone tells the time it does because movement needed everyone to agree, and almost everything built since has been designed to take time out of the journey.

The shorter word for this is speed. French philosopher and urbanist Paul Virilio, who approached the subject through architecture, spent a career arguing that speed is a political arrangement rather than a technical fact. We live less in a democracy, he wrote, than in a dromocracy: the reign of speed. Yet if speed is a political decision, then pace is something that was decided, and anything that was decided can be decided differently. This chapter is an account of the people doing exactly that.

Airports and railway stations are being rebuilt as places with a reason to linger, reversing a century of infrastructure meant only to push crowds through. Inside the vehicle, the engine no longer dictates the form around it, turning the cabin into a room—an idea now spilling off the road into campers, floating homes, and habitats untethered from land altogether. Cities are reclaiming lanes from cars and handing them back to pedestrians; trains are running slowly on purpose again; transit is being drawn for bodies it was never meant to hold; and the corridors that highways once severed are being stitched back together for the wildlife that used them first.

illustration by [Philippos Avramides](https://www.behance.net/philavramides) © designboom

The promise in contrapposto is a step that never arrives. Nauman’s contribution was to finally take it, awkwardly, for an hour, discovering in the process a body and a room he had not quite met before. States of Motion looks into that same interval: the uneasy, productive space between deciding to move another way, figuring out how to do it, and experiencing what takes shape when we actually do.

items.body:
Last week, the AI company Anthropic went public in what became the largest IPO in American history. Given my sustained criticism of Anthropic’s beliefs and actions, many people have asked me for my opinion on this event.

The good news for the curious among you is that I captured my thoughts in an op-ed for *The New York Times*, which they published Thursday, the same day that Anthropic went public. It was titled “[Don’t Play Anthropic’s Game](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/opinion/anthropic-ipo-ai-regulation.html),” and it opens as follows:

“By the close of the stock market today, Anthropic will have become a central pillar of the American economy. This is deeply concerning to me, because it’s unclear how many of the retail and institutional investors handing over their money to Anthropic realize that they are, in some sense, funding a doomsday cult that also happens to build enterprise software.”

My use of “doomsday cult” isn’t facetious; it underscores a critical reality. As many have reported ([including myself](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/05/opinion/ai-silicon-valley.html)), the leaders of Anthropic have long believed that AI is destined to transform the human species, either delivering a utopia or killing us all. They see themselves, with their highly rational minds, trained on long hours during the 2000s debating these issues on blogs like *Less Wrong* and *Overcoming Bias*, as the select few who must rise up to guide humanity through this next evolution.

This may sound like hyperbole, but it’s not. [It’s exactly what they believe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jt508VjX2H8).

Some ask, “Why is this a problem? If any company is going to advance AI, shouldn’t it be one that cares about bad outcomes?”

As I elaborate in my op-ed, the situation is not so simple. Anthropic’s belief that transformational AI is imminent has made it reckless. Anthropic now releases models faster than they can build safeguards because they believe the fate of the human race depends on getting to superintelligent AI first. (Case in point: earlier this year, they announced they were relaxing rules that required them to slow down development if models became hard to control. Their reason? If they applied such rules “unilaterally,” other – presumably less righteous – parties might get ahead of them in the race.)

Indeed, Anthropic stated a key rationale for their IPO is to raise the money needed to accelerate investments in so-called “recursive self-improvement,” where AI systems upgrade themselves. This is, of course, a terrible idea, as it creates models that are even less safe and harder to understand. Anthropic acknowledged these risks in its S-1 filing, but sees no alternative if they’re to continue as humanity’s shepherd through this revolution.

It’s unclear to what degree they even care about profits or building a durable business. As I summarize in my op-ed:

“It’s a business plan that starts with a lot of red ink and then abruptly ends with superintelligence arriving and rendering money superfluous.”

To be clear: generative AI is an incredibly important technological revolution. It brings with it great promises and real risks. But the right way to navigate these innovations can’t possibly be to let a small number of people in Silicon Valley, who have been worshipping AI as a millenarian agent since well before LLMs entered the scene, gather as much money as possible to fund their self-proclaimed role as prophets who will lead the rest of us to their idiosyncratic vision of a better future.

#### In Other News

For more on the question of whether Amodei and company are right in their beliefs that we’re on a trajectory toward superintelligence, check out [my recent technical article](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-superintelligence-debate) for the *IEEE Spectrum*, which lays out an engineering case against the feasibility of AI superintelligence. (You should also consider signing up for the Spectrum’s always insightful [AI Alert newsletter](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-alert-signup).)

# Neuer Kopfhörer von HEDD - der HEDDphone DX ist da!

## HEDD HEDDphone DX Kopfhörer

## Verbesserter Kopfhörer - auch Upgrade-Kit erhältlich!

HEDD HEDDphone DX Kopfhörer

HEDD Audio kündigt den HEDDphone DX an, einen neuen dynamischen und offenen Kopfhörer. Der DX baut auf dem D1 von HEDD auf, nutzt aber eine neue 50-mm-TPC-Membran (Thin-Ply Carbon Diaphragm) mit hoher Auslenkung, um laut Hersteller tiefe Bässe hinab bis 20 Hz bei vollem Pegel auszugeben. Darüber hinaus soll der HEDD HEDDphone DX eine verfeinerte Höhenwiedergabe und eine breite Stereobühne bieten.

## HEDD HEDDphone DX

Im Zentrum des neuen HEDDphone DX steht ein 50 mm-Treiber mit Thin-Ply-Carbon-Diaphragm-Technologie (TPCD). Die ultradünne, geschichtete Kohlefasermembran verbindet ein geringes Gewicht mit hoher Steifigkeit und zusammen mit einer präzisen Konstruktion soll diese schnelle, kontrollierte Bewegungen über den gesamten Frequenzbereich ermöglichen und dabei unerwünschte Resonanzen reduzieren. Laut HEDD ist eine detailreiche Wiedergabe mit minimalen Verzerrungen und einer differenzierten Darstellung das Ergebnis.

Neben den klanglichen Eigenschaften hat HEDD den Kopfhörer auch beim Thema Tragekomfort weiterentwickelt. Dafür wurde gemeinsam mit Capra Audio ein neuer Federkopfbügel hergestellt. So soll ein elastisches Neoprenband das Gewicht des Kopfhörers von 310 g gleichmäßig über den Kopf verteilen und so auch bei langen Hörsessions für einen stabilen, komfortablen Sitz sorgen.

Ein offener Kapselrücken und lasergravierte Details ergänzen das Design.

Zum Lieferumfang des HEDD HEDDphone DX gehört ein symmetrisches 2,2 m langes OCC-Kabel sowie ein Transportcase mit einer doppelter Schutzhülle.

Wie alle HEDDphone-Modelle wird auch der DX in Berlin montiert und geprüft. Sämtliche Komponenten sind austauschbar, zudem ist optional eine erweiterte 5 Jahres Garantie erhältlich.

Der Kopfhörer ist ab sofort zum Preis von 1.199,- Euro im Handel erhältlich.

Ab Ende Januar 2027 wird dann der aktualisierte D1 mit dem oben beschriebenen neuen Kopfband für 799,- Euro erhältlich sein. Das aktualisierte Modell ist 30 g leichter als der bisherige D1. Besitzer des D1 können sich dann das „Headband Upgrade Kit“ für 99,- Euro zulegen.

Sie sehen gerade einen Platzhalterinhalt von YouTube . Um auf den eigentlichen Inhalt zuzugreifen, klicken Sie auf die Schaltfläche unten. Bitte beachten Sie, dass dabei Daten an Drittanbieter weitergegeben werden.

Mehr Informationen Inhalt entsperren Erforderlichen Service akzeptieren und Inhalte entsperren

items.body: Background: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are increasingly used for health information and emotional support, yet little is known about their use for mental health by university students, a population with high digital literacy and elevated mental health need. Objective: To estimate the prevalence of GenAI use for mental health support among respondents to a survey at a single UK university and to identify demographic and well-being characteristics associated with use. Methods: Cross-sectional online survey of students at a large UK university. The primary outcome was self-reported GenAI use for mental health support in the past 6 months. Well-being was assessed using the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale. Associations were examined using multivariable modified Poisson regression to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios. Results: Of 22,207 students invited, 2020 responded (response rate 9.1%). Among respondents, 25.0% (n=503) reported GenAI use for mental health support in the past 6 months. The most common reasons were advice when emotionally distressed (n=380, 19.3%), insights into mental health (n=256, 12.7%), and using GenAI as a personal therapist or coach (n=173, 8.6%); 2.7% (n=54) reported using GenAI to seek support when experiencing thoughts of self-harm. Use was more common among students aged 26-29 years, those identifying as Asian, students reporting a declared disability, students enrolled in management programs, and those with lower well-being. Conclusions: Among respondents at a UK university, approximately one in four reported using GenAI for mental health support. Use was concentrated among students reporting poorer well-being and disability, suggesting that GenAI may function as an informal help-seeking pathway. Universities and health services should anticipate GenAI as a help-seeking pathway and ensure appropriate guidance, integration with existing services, and safeguards to support safe and equitable use.

items.body:
# Google Gemini bekommt ein Chat-Archiv

## Google Gemini bekommt ein Chat-Archiv

von Benjamin Mamerow 24. Nov. 2026 | 0

Die Seitenleiste von Gemini ist nach geraumer Zeit der Nutzung ziemlich vollgepappt mit Entwürfen, Fragen zur Steuererklärung und allem, was ihr sonst so in der Vergangenheit gefragt habt. Zum Aufräumen gibt es bislang nur die Option des Löschens, dann sind aber auch eventuell noch nützliche Antworten weg. Android Authority hat in der aktuellen Version der Google-App nun eine Funktion zum Archivieren von Chats gefunden .

Ein langer Druck auf einen Eintrag in der Seitenleiste öffnet demnach ein Menü, dort steht dann die Option zum Archivieren. Danach verschwindet der Chat aus der normalen Übersicht, bleibt aber gespeichert. Gemini bekommt einen Filter für archivierte Chats direkt in der Seitenleiste, damit ihr jene dann auch bei Gelegenheit schnell wieder hervorholen könnt.

Im Programmcode steckt noch ein zweiter Eintrag namens Spaces. Hierbei handelt es sich um einen dedizierten Button, ein Klick darauf wechselt in den Aufgaben-Tab und trägt im Textfeld die Aufforderung ein, einen neuen Bereich anzulegen. Mehr passiert aktuell aber nicht, denn auf den Servern von Google fehlt derzeit die dafür nötige Technik. Möglich, dass sich dahinter ein gemeinsamer Arbeitsbereich für Dokumente verbirgt, ähnlich wie bei ChatGPT.

items.body:
Kaleidoscopic [patterns](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/patterns/) adorn the exterior of this [pavilion](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/pavilions-tag/) in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio [Selldorf Architects](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/selldorf-architects/) as an [art gallery.](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/galleries/)

Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the [Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/01/14/museum-of-islamic-art-im-pei-21st-century-architecture/).

### Photographs

Previous

Next

### Photographs

Close

It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter's own work.

Richter designed the Doha Pavilion with[Selldorf Architects](https://www.selldorf.com/) as a reference to his Strip paintings – a series that involved digitally dividing his Abstract Painting artwork into vertical stripes, building on his earlier explorations of colour, pattern and repetition.

"My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work," said Richter.

"The pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the patterns that first led me to the Strips," he continued. "Doha is the right place and the only place for my pavilion.”

Doha Pavilion has a six-sided form, wrapped in psychedelic tiles displaying repeating, kaleidoscopic patterns that recall geometries seen in Islamic art, nodding to the project's context.

Selldorf Architects founder Annabelle Selldorf said the design reflects a "profound culmination of many years of [Richter's] research into abstraction".

"I am grateful for the welcome that Gerhard Richter extended to me, and for the wonderful dialogue that ensued, as my studio made manifest the work that had existed in his mind," she said.

"This pavilion is the profound culmination of many years of his research into abstraction, with intensely physical patterns that invite you to immerse yourself in their endlessness," she continued.

"The more I look at them, the more fascinating they become to me as an architectural space to experience."

Inside, Richter's paintings and sculptures are displayed throughout the hexagonal gallery space. This includes both archival and new works made especially for the pavilion.

Among the new works is the Strip Tower – a freestanding tripartite sculpture.

[Read: David Chipperfield Architects builds concrete gallery around singular artwork in Germany](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/10/20/anselm-kiefer-pavilion-david-chipperfield-architects-germany/)

The opening of Doha Pavilion coincides with the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar 2026, which is an international visual arts quadrennial.

Elsewhere, [Selldorf Architects recently completed the controversial remodel of the National Gallery’s Sainsbury Wing](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/05/06/sainsbury-wing-renovation-national-gallery-selldorf-architects-london/). In an interview with Dezeen after the opening, founder Selldorf said that ["what matters is I know why we did things"](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/05/06/annabelle-selldorf-gallery-renovation-sainsbury-wing-frick-collection-interview/).

items.body:
# One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job

My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional, but might not meet your daily driving needs. It’s tucked away out of view, meant to live out the rest of its life in a drawer before finally being cleaned out and donated the next time someone opens the drawer and asks why you’re holding on to outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren’t hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use.

I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible big-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I quickly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life like so many other forgotten devices in a drawer.

## Installation is a doddle

Getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been any simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as simple as plugging the tablet into my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service so the desktop agent launches after initial login, and even asks if you’d like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device.

I already had developer mode initialized on the tablet, but had to go back and allow ADB over USB in settings. The total installation time from copying the script from the project website to everything running on my PC and tablet was less than a minute. The app is MIT-licensed , works on Android 5.0 or later, and requires sideloading since it is not available on the Google Play Store .

The installation script also prints its own uninstall script before it finishes. So often these days, getting rid of an unwanted app feels more difficult than installing it, so I appreciate the straightforward approach the developer has implemented.

## What your device becomes

The first time you fire PhoneBox up, you get live performance and diagnostic information from your PC, along with several pages of optional content that can be tweaked for your local setup to display information that’s pertinent to your uses.

Where PhoneBox really starts to shine is the widget catalog. A collection of free add-ons that can be added as pages to the tablet’s cycling page layouts. There are more general widgets like RSS feeds that display news highlights from your chosen sources, or simple displays like timers or world clocks.

I opted for a few different widgets that caught my eye. One let me view my library of installed Steam titles and launch them on my PC with a simple tap of the tablet screen. Another allows me to control smart home entities hosted by my Home Assistant server. I was controlling the lights in my office from my tablet within seconds of adding the widget. It’s brilliant.

Setting up additional widgets is as simple as adding them to the page layout from the PC’s web interface and hitting save. As soon as I updated things from the PC, the connected tablet immediately began reflecting the changes. I haven’t had the chance to test most of the 131 current options in the widget catalog, but the ones I did were simple to modify and worked on the first try.

## Some frictions

While I didn’t have any major issues with PhoneBox, I did notice a couple of early annoyances along the way. Windows users should be aware that the PC companion app on that OS is currently unsigned, and they should expect a SmartScreen notification when attempting to install the software.

All control settings live in the web interface rather than the phone or tablet you’re connecting. When I first started messing with PhoneBox, I noticed it displayed my weather location as Tallinn. Nothing against the capital of Estonia, but that’s not weather information that does me much good here in the US Midwest. When I went into the widget settings to change the report location, there was nothing to be found. It turns out that you have to change those settings from the general user preferences section rather than within the widget itself. Not a deal-breaker by any means, but a slight hiccup for someone who was new to the software.

Connecting the Android tablet with my PC over USB was totally painless, but I never got the wireless route to work in my testing. Users are meant to generate a QR code from the PhoneBox web interface on their PC, and connect it to their device by scanning the code with their phone/tablet. Every time I tried to scan the code from my device’s camera app, the tablet refused. There’s no QR scanner built into the PhoneBox app, so if your camera app won’t cooperate, the documented path dead-ends. USB was my intended route anyway and works great, but if you’re planning a wireless-only setup, be prepared for possible friction. The documented flow depends on your device camera opening the pairing link, and mine wasn’t in the mood.

In writing this guide on gift ideas for friends, I learned that there really is no catchall gift that will please everyone. Choosing these gifts, I thought back to some of the best self-care products and tech I’ve tested recently. So please use this guide as a starting point, keeping your friend’s personality, needs, and hobbies in mind as you shop for the right gifts.

After testing hundreds of products during my years on the WIRED Reviews team, these are the items I’d recommend to the friends on my own list. I’ve included self-care gifts like massagers, cozy gifts like an ultrasoft throw blanket, kitchen staples like a chef’s knife, and everything in between. There are many gifts at different price points, and they’re also categorized by gift type below. Be sure to check back often, as I will be updating this guide with versatile new picks as we get closer to gifting season.
