items.body:
# Das Recht, nicht vorhergesagt zu werden

## Das Recht, nicht vorhergesagt zu werden

Künstliche Intelligenz ist eine Prognosetechnologie, die die menschliche Autonomie in Frage stellt. Daher braucht es einen neuen Freiheitsbegriff, meint unser Autor.

Die Agenten sind los: KI-gestützte Assistenten, die für ihre Nutzer E-Mails schreiben, online einkaufen oder Zugtickets buchen, sollen das Leben von Millionen Menschen erleichtern. Statt nach einer Unterkunft auf Mallorca zu googeln, erteilt man einfach einen Suchbefehl. Die KI wühlt sich autonom durch die Angebote und schlägt eine Schneise durch das Informationsdickicht, das auf ein paar Entscheidungsbäume eingedampft wird. Der Nutzer will nicht zehn blaue Links, sondern ein Ergebnis, das für ihn maßgeschneidert ist.

Mittlerweile gibt es eine neue Generation von KI-Agenten wie Meta Muse oder Claude Duet, die nicht nur konkrete Aufträge abarbeiten, sondern proaktiv Handlungen vorschlagen, zum Beispiel unbezahlte Rechnungen überweisen oder Meetings verschieben. Der Nutzer muss diese Aktionen zwar freigeben, doch das Ziel der Kybernetiker im Silicon Valley, den Alltag auf Autopilot zu stellen, rückt damit ein Stück näher. In einem nächsten Schritt könnten die Agenten mit Vollmachten ausgestattet werden. Wer regelmäßig Tierfutter oder Kontaktlinsen benötigt, könnte den KI-Assistenten ermächtigen, in einem bestimmten Intervall das Produkt zu erwerben. Und wenn der Agent aus den Chatverläufen lernt, dass der Nutzer mit dem Kauf eines Ohrrings liebäugelt, könnte er den Schmuck bestellen, wenn er am günstigsten ist.

Amazon hat bereits vor einigen Jahren ein Patent auf ein Liefersystem („anticipatory shipping“) angemeldet, das Waren verschickt, noch bevor der Kunde auf den Bestellknopf drückt. Auf Grundlage von vergangenen Bestellungen, Suchhistorie, Wunschlisten sowie Browsergewohnheiten würde das algorithmengesteuerte Logistiksystem entsprechende Waren verpacken und auf Verdacht in die Nähe des Kunden verfrachten – in lokale Sortierzentren oder, bei entsprechender Kaufwahrscheinlichkeit, schon in den Lieferwagen. Was die Planer im Sozialismus nicht schafften, könnte ausgerechnet Big Data möglich machen: die präzise Vorhersage und Steuerung der Nachfrage.

Mittlerweile ist das Datenmaterial deutlich feinkörniger, und die KI kann Wünsche erkennen, derer sich die Nutzer noch gar nicht bewusst sind. So weiß Spotify anhand der Hörgewohnheiten schon heute, welchen Song Nutzer morgen zu Ende hören oder ihrer Playlist hinzufügen werden. Künstliche Intelligenz ist im Kern eine Prognosetechnologie, die nicht nur die nächsten Buchstaben oder Pixel, sondern auch die nächsten Käufe, Partner oder Einbrüche vorhersagen kann. Ökonomen der Monash University haben in einer Studie („Should I State or Should I Show? Aligning AI with Human Preferences“) herausgefunden, dass KI-Agenten, die mit Entscheidungsdaten aus der Vergangenheit trainiert wurden, die Präferenzen der Probanden genauer vorhersagen können als Agenten, die geschriebene Anweisungen erhielten – was auch damit zu tun hat, dass Menschen Probleme haben, ihre Wünsche zu verbalisieren bzw. zu prompten. Der Wille kommt also besser zur Geltung, wenn das Subjekt nicht selbst kommuniziert, sondern kommuniziert wird.

Das verweist auf einen grundlegenden Strukturwandel der Digitalwirtschaft. In der Aufmerksamkeitsökonomie geht es vor allem darum, Nutzer möglichst lange bei der Stange zu halten und durch visuelle Reize Kaufimpulse zu setzen. Die Intention Economy setzt dagegen einen Schritt vorher an und versucht, die Entscheidungsfindung in einem früheren Stadium zu beeinflussen: den Absichten. „Wir interessieren uns für umfangreiche Datensätze, die die menschliche Gesellschaft widerspiegeln und die derzeit noch nicht ohne Weiteres öffentlich online zugänglich sind“, skizziert die KI-Firma OpenAI auf ihrem Blog ihre Ambitionen. „Besonders suchen wir nach Daten, in denen menschliche Absichten zum Ausdruck kommen – etwa in Form längerer Texte oder Konversationen, statt lediglich unzusammenhängender Fragmente –, unabhängig von Sprache, Thema oder Format.“

Die Cambridge-Forscher Yaqub Chaudhary und Jonnie Penn haben in einem Aufsatz („Beware the Intention Economy: Collection and Commodification of Intent via Large Language Models“) für die „Harvard Data Science Review“ beschrieben, wie mit der Intention Economy ein „digitaler Marktplatz für kommodifzierte Signale der ‚Absicht‘“ entsteht. Bevor wir uns selbst bewusst sind, dass wir einen Flug buchen wollen, könnte die KI Bescheid wissen und unsere Motivationen meistbietend an Anzeigenkunden verkaufen.

Natürlich kann ein KI-Agent nicht mit 100-prozentiger Wahrscheinlichkeit vorhersagen, dass man im nächsten Jahr Tickets für ein Oasis-Konzert kauft. Er kann aber durch den dialogischen Charakter viel mehr als eine Suchmaschine, die ja bloß ein Ticketautomat für Datenautobahnen ist, Präferenzen beeinflussen und Nutzer mittels Nudging, also verhaltenspsychologischer Manipulation, lenken: „Du hast jetzt so oft Oasis gehört und wünschst dir tief in deinem Innern, auf ein Konzert zu gehen, also habe ich schon mal zwei Tickets reserviert.“ Es kommt auch bei großen Sprachmodellen auf die Sprecherposition an: Wenn ein KI-Freund ein Produkt empfiehlt, hat das aufgrund der Intimität der Beziehung ein anderes Gewicht als die unpersönliche Empfehlung eines Fernsehgesichts.

items.body:
Indianola, Texas a coastal town that was once the second largest port in Texas next to at the time Galveston.In 1956 the port received a shipment of camels as part of the United States Camel Corps experiment to replace horses and mules as the primary work animal for southwestern America.

During the Civil War, it was occupied by the Union army, once in 1862, then again a year later. Part of that regiment later drowned moving from Indianola to Matagorda island.

The island was later hit twice again, this time by hurricanes, in 1876 and 1886. The second hurricane was accompanied by a major fire and also submerged most of the town, killing hundreds.

Now basically no sign of the town is left other than a few plaques (one being a marker of where the courthouse used to be). It is however valued as a great spot for fishing for local trout, redfish and flounder.

# Hohe Spritpreise: Kaum Entlastung durch den Tankrabatt

## Hohe Spritpreise : Kaum Entlastung durch den Tankrabatt

Dem Staat entgehen durch das aktuelle Senken der Energiesteuer rund 2,5 Milliarden Euro. Im Mittel kommen davon pro Autohaushalt 13 Euro im Monat an.

24.11.2026

12:21 Uhr

teilen

Diesen Artikel teilen

Auch diese autofahrende Person wird den Tankrabatt vermutlich kaum, die hohen Spritpreise dafür um so mehr im Geldbeutel spüren Foto: Sina Schuldt/dpa

Von

Der Tankrabatt bringt kaum Entlastungen für die Menschen im Land. Dies ist das Ergebnis einer Studie, die das Institut für Makroökonomie und Konjunkturforschung (IMK) der gewerkschaftsnahen Hans-Böckler-Stiftung am Dienstag veröffentlicht hat. Demnach sparte ein Haushalt, der im Besitz eines Verbrenners ist, durch die Maßnahme im Mittel 13 Euro im Monat. Dabei profitierten einkommensstarke Haushalte am meisten.

Der Bundesregierung hat den Tankrabatt als Reaktion auf die im Zuge des Irankriegs gestiegenen Spritpreise eingeführt. In einer frühen Phase galt er zunächst von Mai bis Juni. Der jetzige Tankrabatt gilt seit Oktober bis Jahreswechsel. Durch die Absenkung der Energiesteuer auf Diesel und Benzin sollen die Preise an den Zapfsäulen 17 Cent pro Liter niedriger sein als ohne Rabatt. Die aktuelle Senkung kostet den Staat rund 2,5 Milliarden Euro.

„Der Tankrabatt hat schnell und unmittelbar die Inflationsrate gedämpft. Das war ein wichtiger Effekt“, sagt IMK-Chef Sebastian Dullien. „Er hat allerdings auch eine Reihe von Nachteilen, sodass er für eine langfristige Entlastung bei hohen Energiepreisen nicht ideal ist.“ So kam die Wirkung des Rabattes hauptsächlich bei reichen Autofahrern an. Während sich der Effekt bei Haushalten mit einem Einkommen von maximal 2.000 Euro auf im Mittel 7 Euro im Monat belief, waren es an der Spitze der Einkommensverteilung 19 Euro. Insgesamt entfielen auf das reichste Viertel rund 45 Prozent des gesamten Entlastungsvolumens.

## Ein Drittel spart woanders

Damit ist die Wirkung des Tankrabatts so gering, dass die Menschen sie gar nicht wahrnehmen. 61 Prozent der im Rahmen der IMK-Studie befragten Verbrennerfahrenden gaben an, die Entlastung kaum oder gar nicht zu spüren. Stattdessen spart rund ein Drittel der Befragten wegen der hohen Spritpreise an anderer Stelle.

„Die anhaltende Verunsicherung der Menschen aufgrund der hohen Spritpreise dürfte den privaten Konsum somit zusätzlich belasten“, so die IMK-Forscher. „Insbesondere gezielte Direktzahlungen könnten als Ergänzung zu preisdämpfenden Maßnahmen wie einer Stromsteuersenkung die Kaufkraft einkommensschwacher Haushalte stärken und dazu beitragen, Einschränkungen beim Konsum abzufedern.“

items.body:
Eczema causes itchy, inflamed rashes on the skin

Evgeniia Gordeeva/Getty Images

Over a third of people with moderate to severe eczema taking part in a clinical trial have seen their skin completely or almost completely clear up after taking an experimental pill for four months. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected.

“It definitely looks promising,” says [Gayle Ross](https://www.thermh.org.au/our-people/gayle-ross) at the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

[Read more Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2491017-chronic-inflammation-messes-with-your-mind-heres-how-to-calm-it/)

Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13.

In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is [effective](https://www.dupixenthcp.com/atopicdermatitis/efficacy-safety/adult-real-world-results), it has had [limited uptake](https://www.sciencedirect.com/org/science/article/pii/S256209592300065X) in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage.

Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema.

Free newsletter

#### Sign up to Health Check

[Sign up to newsletter](https://www.newscientist.com/sign-up/health/)

In the [clinical trial](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07217015), 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks.

Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average [72 per cent reduction](https://investors.kymeratx.com/news-releases/news-release-details/kymera-therapeutics-announces-positive-results-broaden2-phase-2b) in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared to 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial.

“These results exceeded our expectations,” said [Terence Rooney](https://www.kymeratx.com/about-us/leadership/terence-rooney-md/), the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a [webcast](https://investors.kymeratx.com/news-releases/news-release-details/kymera-therapeutics-announces-positive-results-broaden2-phase-2b) on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end.

“It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross.

[Read more You can upgrade your immune system, but not in the way you think](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2507511-you-can-upgrade-your-immune-system-but-not-in-the-way-you-think/)

The medication also appeared safe. A small proportion of participants developed conjunctivitis as a side-effect, but it tended to be mild and didn’t cause anyone to discontinue treatment, said Rooney. In fact, since the trial, almost every participant has chosen to continue taking the daily pill as part of an ongoing study, he said.

People taking dupilumab can develop conjunctivitis too, so “we’re pretty used to dealing with that”, says Ross.

Kymera Therapeutics is now planning a larger trial of KT-621 for treating eczema that is scheduled to begin in mid-2027. The company is also currently running a [trial of KT-621 in people with asthma](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07323654), since the condition is caused by the same overactive immune pathway operating in the lungs. It hasn’t yet said how much the drug will cost if it eventually receives regulatory approval.

items.subtitle: In an article about AI and human nature in The Free Press (AI Will Change What It Is To Be Human.

Humans have been, the authors claim, the smartest beings around for all of our history. But that will change with the development of artificial intelligence. And this will lead to what the authors call an identity crisis: no human will be able to compete with artificial intelligence on the…
items.body:
**by Marianne Janack**

In an article about AI and human nature in The Free Press ([AI Will Change What It Is To Be Human. Are We Ready?](https://www.thefp.com/p/ai-will-change-what-it-is-to-be-human?utm_source=publication-search)) Tyler Cowen and Avital Balwit predict that artificial intelligence, like many technological advances before it, can improve human life, but that it can also challenge our very ideas about what it is to be human. Humans have been, the authors claim, the smartest beings around for all of our history. But that will change with the development of artificial intelligence. And this will lead to what the authors call an identity crisis: no human will be able to compete with artificial intelligence on the basis of intelligence. The authors predict that we will value other kinds of things: people who do physical labor or work in the energy sector; people who provide inspiration (coaches and mentors) or entertainment. Greeters, charmers, and flatterers will also be in demand, Balwit and Cowen argue, if only to satisfy what they see as the human biological need for obsequiousity and interaction with other humans.

The authors also predict that AI will lead to longer human lives and better health; a boom in participation in human group activities like religious services, clubs, and volunteering; and more and better leisure time. However, along with these benefits might come a heavy dose of demoralization. If what we value is our intelligence and intellectual work, then AI will be better at those things than we are. It will make us obsolete if we are primarily knowledge workers. If we extol the virtues of intellectual humility, charisma, making friends, and pursuing things that we think of as meaningful, however, we can avoid the demoralization that will come if we continue to value intelligence. Human life will change, but the authors are not worried: “Humans are remarkably adaptable. We foraged and farmed, we built factories and spaceships, we wrote prayers, plays, poems, novels, and code. And now? Now we created this,” they say. So why should we think that AI will change human nature?

The language of human nature seems to suggest that we are not adaptable. We crave hierarchy, status, and connection to others, according to Balwit and Cowen. It seems that AI will not change these facts about us. Instead of finding status in being smart, getting good grades, or owning expensive things, however, we might find that we seek status in having friends or being humble. But, they warn, this is not the only possible outcome: we also might find that we compete more with others on the basis of physical strength, physical attributes, or on the quality of our AI companions. Our cravings are part of our natures, but how we satisfy those cravings is adaptable. Our future measures of status might look as strange to us now as our present measures might have looked to a person living 300 years ago, the authors say. There are a number of different ways the future might turn out.

Some of this is a debate about nature vs. nurture: how much of what we do is innate and how much is learned? Are we blank slates? Or do we come pre-programmed? Many people have claimed that this is a false dichotomy: that humans might have some characteristics from “nature” that are only potentially expressed, and that “nurture” interacts with “nature” to both elicit that which is natural and, sometimes, to create the natural.

To say that something has a nature is to characterize it as having predictable dispositions to respond in certain ways to repeatable situations. The nature of water is captured both by what it does in a given set of situations and what it is (H2O), with the former being ideally explainable by the latter. But human nature? What is the nature of humans? Are humans different from other things, like animals and machines, that might share some of our dispositions?

The classic response to this question since Aristotle pondered it has been that humans are ‘rational animals’—we are mortal, but we also have the ability to reason. Aristotle actually said that human beings are *zōon logon echon* —beings possessing *logos*; beings that can both reason and use language. These abilities were captured by subsequent theorists as ‘rationality’. But using the possession of rationality as definitive of human nature just seems to defer the theoretical problem. Is rationality reflected in language use? In the ability to think about our own thinking? To think in terms of universals and abstract terms? Often, rationality is glossed as intelligence, and in that case it’s something that can be measured by IQ tests, and represented as an ability to remember and store information. This is the sense in which Balwit and Cowen seem to understand rationality, and if AI is smarter than humans, our claim to rationality is, they assume, also threatened.

In his writings about anthropology, Immanuel Kant said that the greatest concern of human beings is what one must do in order to be a human being—suggesting that the human being is not a being that can be understood independently of what matters to her—and that being a human being is less about what is innate than about what we can become. Unlike the objects of empirical science, like water or rocks, our nature is tied up with what we value and what we strive for. And yet, as Balwit and Cowen suggest, our ideas about what it is to be human must be responsive to a world in which humans are not as smart as the technology we’ve created. The world we have created, they argue, is a world in which human beings might feel demoralized because we are no longer the smartest thing in existence.

…

items.title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
items.subtitle: Need for speed: Data center developers are bypassing years-long grid connection waits by building their own private natural gas power plants.
items.feedText: Over 100 such facilities have been announced in the US since early 2025, with combined capacity exceeding 115 gigawatts. A dirtier shortcut: If all planned US projects proceed, they could emit 152 million metric tons more CO₂ annually than if those data centers were grid connected, according to BloombergNEF tracking. Fossil fuel lock-in is a real risk: Though developers pitch private gas plants as temporary bridges until grid connections come through, experts warn that once built, operators are unlikely to simpl…
items.body:
# Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

Or are our experiences of mental distress culturally specific? by Alexander Pereira + BIO Subway station in People’s Square, Shanghai, China, 2011. Photo by Carlos Barria/Reuters Listen to this essay 29 minute listen On a November day in 1994, a 14-year-old girl in Hong Kong named Charlene Hsu Chi-Ying collapsed on a busy sidewalk, in broad daylight, in her school uniform.
items.body:
# Are mental illnesses universal, or are they culturally specific?

## Is mental illness universal?

## Do all cultures experience the same mental disorders? Or are our experiences of mental distress culturally specific?

Subway station in People’s Square, Shanghai, China, 2011. Photo by Carlos Barria/Reuters

Listen to this essay

29 minute listen

On a November day in 1994, a 14-year-old girl in Hong Kong named Charlene Hsu Chi-Ying collapsed on a busy sidewalk, in broad daylight, in her school uniform. She had starved herself to death. Charlene had never been diagnosed with anorexia, not because her self-starvation went unnoticed, but because the diagnosis, in its Western form, was mostly unknown in the East. Her death changed that overnight. Splashed across the front pages were stark headlines such as ‘Girl Who Died In Street Was A Walking Skeleton’.

Local journalists scrambled for an explanation of this tragedy, and quickly found a template ready-made: a Western account of what anorexia was, what it felt like, who got it, what caused it. The ideas spread rapidly – particularly that anorexia involved distorted self-perceptions about one’s body (dysmorphia) and an intense, borderline delusional, fear of gaining weight, often cued by prevailing beauty standards (notably, a cultural fixation with slender female bodies). Mass public education campaigns followed. Hotlines opened, celebrities spoke out. Anorexia became part of the zeitgeist.

Before Charlene’s death, the psychiatrist Sing Lee had been quietly studying a small number of women in Hong Kong who were starving themselves to dangerous degrees. Most of these women did not obsess over their bodies, nor fear becoming fat. They instead complained of somatic (bodily) ailments: uncomfortable bloating, a profound lack of appetite. The cognitive hallmark of Western anorexia – a distorted body image – was largely absent. Lee seemed to be documenting a distinct form of self-starvation with its own local logic. The situation has changed dramatically since then. By 2007, more than three-quarters of the anorexic patients Lee treated cited ‘fat phobia’ as a central motivation. Today, anorexia in Hong Kong is terrifyingly common, affecting roughly one in 200 schoolgirls – comparable to trends in the United States.

We do not know the form that Charlene’s illness took. What we do know is that her death became a catalyst for the rapid importation of a Western conceptual framework that reshaped how Hong Kong understood and experienced disordered eating in young women.

Anorexia is just one example from a compendium of curious cases in which culture seemingly shapes mental disorders. For example, anthropologists have documented how cultures sculpt ‘idioms of distress’ – socially learned and sanctioned ways of communicating unusual mental episodes and patterns of psychological suffering. Hallucinations and dissociative states are routinely interpreted as forms of spiritual possession across the globe, as with Zār in northeast Africa and the Middle East.

These cases are not fringe oddities. Even depression – arguably the most common psychiatric condition in the world – seems to look strikingly different depending on when and where it appears. In China, patients who meet Western criteria for depression present mainly with bodily symptoms, such as fatigue, insomnia and headaches, rather than psychological symptoms, like low self-esteem and apathy. Delusions , multiple personality and social anxiety also take different forms in different cultures.

Cultural variation in psychiatry raises fundamental and increasingly urgent questions about abnormal minds. What precisely can culture shape? We usually think of mental disorder as something going wrong inside a person, and of culture as shaping how that internal problem is expressed and socially understood. Can culture penetrate deeper, to reshape the internal problem itself? What would that even look like?

T he suggestion that cultural variables can significantly shape the internal mechanisms of mental disorders, including brute neurobiological hardware, may seem counterintuitive, even radical. But I’ll make the case that culture may possess a more substantial ability to do so – in some disorders, to some degrees – than is generally acknowledged. The basic reason is that the brain, the organ of the mind, is plastic and has functions of representing and adapting to a rich social world.

This could well allow cultural ecosystems to inculcate ‘local’ kinds of disorders – ones that may look similar to their cross-cultural counterparts, but differ in their psychological and even neurological profiles in ways consequential for scientific classification and treatment. ‘Anorexia’ or ‘depression’ in one cultural context may then be best understood as a different condition altogether in another. Mental disorders are already notoriously heterogeneous: one study of 3,703 patients diagnosed with depression found 1,030 distinct combinations of symptoms. One source of this variation may be cultural environments, including subcultures within a country’s borders. These possibilities hinge on unsettled questions about how plastic the mechanisms of mental disorders really are, and whether cultural factors have the right kind of causal access to them.

To begin, let me distinguish three widely accepted ways that culture can shape mental disorders, before investigating whether it can also shape their internal mechanisms. When I say ‘culture’, I mean a broad class of sociocultural factors, including social roles, norms, values, institutional and political structures, even particular medical beliefs and practices. By ‘shape’, I mean causally influence.

Hearing God speak seems a textbook case of psychosis. Yet many US evangelicals cultivate the experience

…

items.body:
Get ready stargazers! The full "Beaver supermoon" rises in the eastern sky, offering up a spectacular display shortly after sunset tonight (Nov. 24). Here's what you need to know.

November's full moon occurs at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk passes opposite the sun in our sky, making it appear fully lit from our perspective. [The November full moon](https://www.space.com/stargazing/november-full-moon-2026-when-where-and-how-to-see-the-beaver-moon) is often referred to as the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the small mammals are hard at work building their lodges in preparation for the winter.

The Beaver Moon is also set to be a dazzling [supermoon](https://www.space.com/supermoon-what-is-it-2026), because it turns full as the natural satellite passes within [90% of perigee](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/resources/teachable-moment/whats-a-supermoon-and-just-how-super-is-it/), when it is at its closest to [Earth](https://www.space.com/54-earth-history-composition-and-atmosphere.html) in its 27-day elliptical orbit. A supermoon's proximity can make it appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than the most distant [full moon](https://www.space.com/16830-full-moon-calendar.html) of the year, which is colloquially known as a "micro-moon".

## When to see the Beaver Moon

November's full moon will be below the horizon for stargazers in the U.S. at the moment it turns full. Instead, viewers in America should look out for the moon shortly after sunset on Nov. 24, as it looms low over the eastern horizon.

A supermoon can make for a spectacular sight when caught close to the horizon. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech)

Try covering the lunar disk with your thumb to block out the worst of its glare, and you may just be able to spot to blue-white lights of the Pleiades open star cluster glimmering less than 10 degrees away — roughly the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length.

If you miss the full moon on Nov. 24, don't worry as [the moon](https://www.space.com/55-earths-moon-formation-composition-and-orbit.html) will appear full to the casual observer for a couple more nights, so there's no excuse to miss it! Remember to check out [Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker](https://www.timeanddate.com/moon/usa/new-york) for timings specific to your location.

## What should I expect from the November supermoon?

You may see the moon turn a striking orange-yellow hue as it rises because sunlight reflected from its disk passes through more of Earth's atmosphere, which scatters shorter bluer wavelengths of light and allows more red and orange light to reach our eyes in a process called Rayleigh scattering.

Celestron Nexstar 4SE

(Image credit: Celestron)

This is a fantastic go-to [telescope](https://www.space.com/15693-telescopes-beginners-telescope-reviews-buying-guide.html)with a 4-inch aperture and can help you quickly find a steady view of the moon. Check out our full [Celestron Nexstar 4SE review](https://www.space.com/celestron-nexstar-4se-telescope-review) for more.

The supermoon will also appear particularly large while close to the horizon, as a phenomenon called the "[moon illusion](https://www.space.com/31287-giant-moon-illusion-all-in-your-head.html)" tricks our brains into thinking that the lunar disk is larger while in the presence of foreground objects compared to when it is overhead.

It'll make for a breathtaking photo opportunity, which you can capitalize on with our [beginner's guide to imaging the full moon](https://www.space.com/how-to-photograph-the-moon-camera), along with our picks of the [best cameras](https://www.space.com/best-cameras-for-astrophotography) and [lenses for capturing the night sky](https://www.space.com/best-lenses-for-astrophotography).

**Editor's Note:** *If you take a photo of the November full moon and would like to share it with Space.com's readers, then please send your photos and comments, along with your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.*

items.body:
A reader who asked to remain anonymous (seriously) pointed me to an [article](https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/say-goodbye-to-anonymous-posting?) about the impending end of anonymous writing.

Large language models are getting increasingly good at identifying the authors of human-written text. In a preprint, “[Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26216),” a team of authors claim that:

> Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer “who wrote this?” at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who.

The authors asked LLMs to provide the identity of different kinds of often-anonymous writing, such as peer reviews and internet comments.

Their findings:

> The best-performing model we test is Claude Fable 5.2, which names the reviewer of 56% of private peer reviews and the username behind 31% of recent Reddit comments.

It appears that your writing is more likely to be outed as yours if some previous writing of yours was in an LLM’s training data, or if you a lot of your writing is available online. And once a model becomes familiar with you, your writing is very likely to be identified as yours:

> Even when a text is brand new, a model can identify its writer from what it learned about them elsewhere; i.e., once that knowledge is in the weights, the writer cannot do anything about it. This leaves people with the largest public footprints, such as active social media users or established authors, permanently exposed, since paraphrasing the text does not completely remove the deanonymization risk. Moreover, the set of vulnerable writers expands as models improve… Maintaining anonymity is especially important for peer review. Our private lab review data comes from only six writers, but a study across thousands of private peer reviews is underway.

Having an AI disguise your writing style by paraphrasing your writing does diminish its recognizability somewhat, but not entirely, the researchers report.

One commenter on the paper, Kelsey Piper, [writes](https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/say-goodbye-to-anonymous-posting?), “We’re witnessing a total erosion of the ability to write anonymously online,” though “the process is still incomplete. Not everyone should consider themselves deanonymized yet. But the erosion is happening.”

Regarding peer review, she writes:

> [T]he institution of anonymous peer review does not look like it will hold up any longer. The space of possible reviewers for a given academic article review in a particular discipline is pretty small; stylistic tics are sufficient to confidently distinguish between them.

Suppose the LLMs get quite a bit better at identifying the authors of anonymous text. What would that mean for the future of peer review? Well, while some reviewers have regularly opted to forgo anonymity, that is typically a privilege exercised by the relatively senior and secure members of the profession. I wouldn’t expect many more to join their ranks. Nor would I expect academia to be content relying on the forbearance of, say, curious authors or grant judges, to preserve anonymity.

There are [alternatives to peer review](https://dailynous.com/2022/02/07/why-a-crowd-sourced-peer-review-system-would-be-good-for-philosophy-guest-post/). Will the erosion of anonymity push more branches of academia to embrace these alternatives?

Or will it be a reason to use AIs even more in academia, say, as peer reviewers? After all, recently [one set of researchers found that](https://gking.harvard.edu/files/peerless.pdf):

> AI-generated article reviews are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts and judged to be of unusually high quality by journal editors and authors.

The study was performed on quantitative social science papers, not philosophy papers, but of course this technology is only a few years old; who knows how it might develop, and how rapidly.

Discussion welcome.

# At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix

Carbon Captured

## At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix

## Amid a bitter standoff over how to stop global warming and pay for its damages, oil-producing nations blocked mention of phasing out fossil fuels, instead pressing to expand carbon capture technology.

A United Nations-sponsored negotiation on climate change collapsed Sunday amid bitter standoffs over how to slow the warming of the planet and who will pay for it. During the two-week summit, oil- and gas-producing nations blocked any mention of phasing out those fuels — a step scientists uniformly agree is a prerequisite to addressing global warming.

Instead, petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, pushed for an aggressive expansion of carbon capture technology as a way to reduce the pollution their fuels cause.

Today, carbon capture facilities operate at a tiny fraction of the scale promised, are riddled with failures and setbacks, and show no signs of being able to overcome those hurdles at the pace that the U.N. suggests would be needed to mitigate global warming, reporting by Drilled and ProPublica has found.

The role of carbon capture was just one cause of discord in Turkey at the 31st annual U.N. climate summit, known as the Conference of the Parties. But it reflects a culmination of decades of effort by fossil fuel companies, and the nations most dependent on them, to slow a transition away from oil, coal and gas in part by pressing for methods like carbon capture, which theoretically allow for the use of their products and cleaning up carbon pollution at the same time.

Over the course of two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, drafts of the summit’s main political accord were stripped of language encouraging such a transition even as specific targets were added to expand carbon capture and storage, or CCS.

One draft released Nov. 16 included language encouraging a transition from fossil fuels alongside a recommendation to scale up carbon capture — where greenhouse gases are caught from industry, or filtered from the air, and injected underground — so that it removes at least 500 million tons of carbon dioxide a year by 2035.

Currently, however, the carbon capture industry buries only a sliver of that amount and has struggled for three decades to meet even the lowest-end projections, leading many climate experts to conclude that it will never be a practical solution to climate change.

“The effort by bad faith petrostate actors to block any agreement at #COP31 on fossil fuel phaseout in favor of (hypothetical future) carbon capture is the best evidence yet that moral hazard FUNDAMENTALLY compromises carbon capture as a climate solution,” wrote Michael Mann, a prominent climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, in a Bluesky post Sunday.

As it stands, most CCS is used to squeeze additional oil from aging fields, so critics say setting global goals for it would lead to further subsidy of oil production, rather than limit or reduce the amount of CO2 that reaches the air.

Behind the scenes in Antalya, some 700 carbon capture lobbyists were registered as attending, up from 531 at last year’s summit in Brazil and more than the combined delegations of all 14 Pacific Small Island Developing States, according to an analysis of U.N. participant lists by the Center for International Environmental Law. Forty-five of those representatives were granted entry to closed-door negotiating sessions. The center has not completed a similar analysis of lobbyists for other technologies.

The agreement — and its emphasis on CCS — “really had the fossil fuel industry’s fingerprints all over it,” said Romain Ioualalen, the global policy lead for the nonprofit Oil Change International, a research and advocacy group pushing for a phaseout of fossil fuels.

A coalition of nations, including the European Union, rejected the proposal outright.

For years, tensions at the annual climate talks have tended to break down to three camps: Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states — at times with tacit U.S. support — which argue for an approach that prioritizes slow changes in the energy system in service of economic stability; the wealthy, industrialized nations, which push for an energy transition but resist measures to pay for both the transition and damages caused by warming; and the low- and middle-income nations, which will sign on to fossil fuel phaseout only if other powerful economies commit to supporting the cost of their transition.

Carbon capture remains just one part of that larger debate, which included other ways to clean up energy sources. But its weight in this year’s talks reflects long-standing efforts to tie climate action to its success, as well as a failure to enact any other meaningful agreement that would slow the rate of CO2 emissions in the first place.

For more than a year, ProPublica and Drilled have investigated the history of carbon capture and storage and the decades-long effort by oil companies to validate it in the scientific community and at the U.N. Our reporting has found that industry funding contributed to influential CCS research at universities, petrostates pressed the U.N. to validate the technology without supporting evidence and climate modelers have assumed it can work at an enormous scale, despite the technology’s troubled real-world track record.

In the closing session, a delegate from Panama explained that the country could not support the language in the final COP31 text in part because “it wagers too much” on CCS “instead of calling for deep changes.”

Vanuatu, a small island nation in the Pacific that is especially vulnerable to rising sea levels, warned that the text “risks legitimizing continued fossil fuel dependence” and that carbon capture must not become “an excuse to prolong the fossil fuel era.”

…

items.body:
# Cassiopeia Production Suite 1 Bundle

Reviews » Gear/Software » Cassiopeia Production Suite 1 Bundle Cassiopeia Production Suite 1 Bundle Share Facebook Twitter WhatsApp These four Kontakt instruments from Soundsphat deliver thousands of highly editable, release-ready presets. Let’s see what sample-based sound design has to offer your productions.

Software synthesizers completely revolutionized the way music was made, and the sound of almost every genre of music has changed as a result. But arguably at least as influential to the music we hear today were sample-based instruments, such as those made for NI’s Kontakt.

From meticulously recreated playable orchestras to special effects and sound design tools, everybody with a computer can produce more complex, modulatable tones in seconds than the entire BBC Radiophonic Workshop could manage in decades.

But with so many analogue-modelled soft synths on the market today, it feels like we rarely use sampled instruments for our core sounds. Which is where the Cassiopeia bundle of Kontakt instruments comes in.

Guided by Grammy-nominated Christian Beat Hirt, Soundsphat aims to deliver a definitive selection of production-ready presets, complete with performance and modulation options, and all of the envelope, filter, and effects controls you could desire.

## Production Suite 1 Overview

There are four instruments in the package: Cassiopeia, Landlord Stabs, Zerotone 6, and The Riga Piano. Each has its own sonic concept but all share a similar interface and layer-based approach to sound design, so we’ll devote most of this review to the headline instrument, Cassiopeia, then explain how the others each riff on this concept.

Cassiopeia is based around four sound layers. The first two play host to the core sound layers like multisampled analogue synth layers, custom wavetables, acoustic-instrument-sourced waveforms, and more. The second two are sound-design-focused layers, including everything from bird calls and bells to subs and metal clangs. You can even add your own layers.

In terms of content, the headline figures are pretty impressive: a 422 GB library size (compressed to around 350 GB on your drive) with 58,000 samples, 120 custom wavetables, and 3,922 multisampled patches.

The sound design is top-notch throughout and the biggest selling point of this package by far. You could absolutely make complete, great-sounding tracks with nothing more than the sounds on offer here. Every kind of patch is covered, from basses and leads to pads and effects. And they’re incredibly polished, rich, slathered in effects, and ready to use.

For all that variety, though, this collection does very much have a distinct vibe. And it’s aimed squarely at the dancefloor and energetic playlists, so if you don’t like those kinds of sounds, this probably won’t be your bag.

## Cassiopeia In Use

Once you’ve found your sounds there is a powerful range of editing options.

The main interface is fairly uncomplicated with an X-Y modulation matrix for simultaneous real-time modulation of multiple effects and some headline parameters such as pitch bend range, filter cutoff and resonance, tone, volume, and velocity sensitivity. Plus buttons to add/mute each of the four sound layers that make up a Cassiopeia patch.

There are then six editing pages. EDIT offers up various controls. For example, polyphony, portamento, and a chord maker feature. Then you can apply up to nine effects: Reverb/convolution, Room, Comp, Delay, EQ, Tape, Chorus, Flanger, and Phaser, with detailed controls for each.

Next comes ADSR, offering up assignable envelope control for volume, cutoff, and pitch of each individual layer. This is very welcome, but unfortunately brings us to the first of only two gripes about this synth. The way you assign the envelopes to the layers is really unintuitive, and hard to understand even after reading the manual. You use the same on/off button to assign a voice to an envelope group as you do to call up that voice’s individual envelope settings. It’s definitely worth revisiting in an update.

Speaking of which, the LFO page has the same sound-shaping benefits and confusing assignment system as ADSR.

Luckily the ARP window is not confusing at all, offering a powerful and intuitive step-sequence-style programmer and all of the swing and timing controls you’d hope for. There’s even a randomize function.

It’s no surprise, then, that some of the most satisfying patches in the whole instrument are found in the ARP preset category – there’s just something fundamentally usable about them, enhanced by the top-tier sound design of each patch. Just keep an eye on the timing as you’ll find most arp-based patches need between −5 and −20 ms of track delay to slot into a project.

The MIX window comes next, with level and pan controls for each of the four layers, plus individual per-layer controls for things like pitch (semitones and cents), high- and low-pass filters, and Body and Silk (for boosting or easing low-mid and high-mid frequencies, respectively).

The layer-based architecture of Cassiopeia patches means you’ll probably spend a lot of time in this window, and it’s powerful and well laid out. It’s a shame, then, that there’s some real jank to the level fader controls – it can be really hard to get hold of them with the mouse pointer, particularly if you’ve previously pulled one all the way down.

Finally, there’s SOUND MENU, which allows you to swap different sound layers in or out. The options for each layer are neatly labelled and categorized, so if you’re the experimental type you’ll find hundreds of options allowing for many thousands of permutations.

## What About The Rest Of The Bundle?

items.body:
# Hakeem Jeffries Can Live With “Medicare for More”

After years of being able to hide behind Republicans’ blatant mismanagement and intentional sabotage of the healthcare system, Democrats will now have to put forth their own plan to save our crumbling healthcare infrastructure. Whether the party can agree on what that plan is remains to be seen.

The middle path has been dubbed “Medicare for More.” It’s been framed variously as a first step toward Medicare for All and as a half-measure to relieve the pressure to pass the more expansive healthcare agenda. Now backed by Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the presumed next speaker of the House, the policy would lower the eligibility age for the public retiree health system; expand dental, vision, and hearing care; and provide universal coverage for children.

> “We’re in the wealthiest nation on Earth, and we’re running out of excuses for why Americans don’t have universal healthcare.”

But the plan would maintain the status quo for people ages 26 to 55 — many of whom saw their Affordable Care Act healthcare premiums spike after December 2025, when enhanced subsidies expired for an estimated 22 million people as a result of Republicans ’ so-called Big, Beautiful Bill.

“We’re in the wealthiest nation on Earth, and we’re running out of excuses for why Americans don’t have universal healthcare,” Rep. Summer Lee, D-Penn., wrote in a statement to the Intercept. “The mandate from voters is change. The American people literally cannot afford to return to the status quo.”

Most Read An Air Force Major Is Being Held in Solitary Confinement for Criticizing Trump on CNN Seth Stern ICE Spreads Misinformation About Securing Your iPhone. Here’s How to Really Do It. Noah Hurowitz, Nikita Mazurov, Karl Loftus Elon Musk Thinks You’re an Idiot Katherine Krueger

Progressives have vowed to pass Medicare for All, a sweeping proposal to establish a national public health insurance program

Polling suggests broad support for Medicare for All, particularly among Democratic voters. A Kaiser Family Foundation poll found that 94 percent of registered Democrats support the policy — and roughly 79 percent of all adults polled favor the federal government doing more to help provide health insurance.

Despite Medicare for All’s growing popularity, Jeffries, a New York Democrat, remained skeptical of the policy throughout the midterms. In August, he told “Meet the Press” that he did not support it, emphasizing that since joining leadership he has declined to co-sponsor Medicare for All legislation.

## Related

### Luigi, a Year Later: How to Build a Movement Against Parasitic Health Insurance Giants

Jayapal, who has reintroduced her signature legislation every session since 2019 and plans to do so again in the next Congress, said wins from candidates who ran on Medicare for All in this year’s midterm elections have helped to push leadership on this issue. She specifically cited the success of purple-state candidates like Sen.-elects Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, who invoked the policy again and again on the campaign trail — and won.

At a meeting of the Congressional Progressive Caucus last week, the Washington congresswoman said that Jeffries agreed to two out of three of the caucus’s requests on Medicare for All. First, he agreed to support the initial phase-in of the Medicare for All Act, which Jayapal says she has been pushing him on for “the last couple of months.” The plan would greatly expand access to healthcare for most Americans by simultaneously lowering the Medicare eligibility age and covering everyone under the age of 18.

Second, he agreed to get a Congressional Budget Office score on the full Medicare for All act. The CBO score estimates the cost of any given legislation, which gives members a chance to weigh the financial impact of a bill before casting their vote.

But Jeffries declined to support their third request: a markup of the full “Medicare for All” bill in committee. Markups allow committees to make amendments to a bill before it gets voted on in front of the full House — making it substantially easier to pass.

Still, Jayapal believes there is a path forward for her bill. She said that she has spoken with both new members and incumbents “who haven’t been on it before” and now say they want to co-sponsor the bill, and she believes that with more of the caucus’s support, Jeffries could support a bill markup in the future.

It appears that attacks on the policy have become less effective with voters over time. Private insurance companies have long supported anti-Medicare for All messaging, Jayapal pointed out.

Opponents of the public healthcare proposal argue it will create longer wait times, raise taxes, and separate people from their preferred doctors. But as the state of healthcare in the United States has degraded and become more dystopian, Jayapal said, “none of those attacks work when people are already experiencing $20,000 in premiums, when they’re already being told they can’t have care by an AI model or by a private insurance company.”
